Home › News and Business › News Makers
Hubbard Radio’s WTOP(FM) has been one of the top revenue-generating stations in the United States for more than a decade, according to BIA estimates. Although it is in Nielsen Market No. 8, it regularly beats out stations in the larger markets to pull off that feat.
WTOP’s over-the-air revenue in 2023, the most recent for which BIA published estimates, was $66.3 million. WTOP led the BIA list 13 times over the previous 14 years. It also pulls in consistently high ratings.
That remarkable streak occurred under the leadership of Joel Oxley, president/GM of WTOP, WFED(AM), the Federal News Network and the 2060 Digital Washington platform.
Oxley, who is about to retire, has been named to receive the 2026 NAB National Radio Award from the National Association of Broadcasters .
We asked him about the uniqueness of the Washington market, changes in newsroom workflows and his secret to generating revenue. Text has been edited for length and clarity.
Radio World: Are you optimistic about the radio broadcast business model going forward?
Joel Oxley: Yes, I think it can still work, but I think you’ve got to have great products, and you must have products that connect to people. You’ve also got to understand that radio is great distribution still. But you’ve got to be playing in all the platforms. As long as you do that, radio can be still a great part of the business.
But it’s not the 1990s anymore. You’ve got to be looking at the business model differently. You can’t be sitting around waiting for agency avails — I mean it’s great when you get agency avails, we love agencies when they call us and give us a bit of business. [But] you have to be incredibly proactive and make sure that you’re getting out and figuring out what you can do to help solve your clients’ needs.
Find solutions. It could be digital. It might not be over the air radio every time.
RW: Does AM have a future as the margins continue to shrink?
Oxley: That’s really going to be market-dependent, signal-dependent. It’s getting harder. I don’t think anybody would tell you that it’s an easy business. We have found some good uses for our AMs, and I think others can too.
Especially when AMs are paired with translators, especially smaller markets, they make a whole hell of a lot of sense.
We’ve experimented with AM digital. There are ways to make AM sound better. There can still be a place for it. But I’m not going to tell you that it’s an easy business.
RW: What makes the Washington radio market unique?
Oxley: I tell people: It’s always a good thing to be in the all-news business in the news capital of the world.
The market has really grown, too. It wasn’t that long ago, honestly, that it was a 2-million-person market. Now it’s over 6 million. If you throw in Baltimore, it’s like 9.
Also the growth of the federal government has meant a lot more jobs have come here. All kinds of government contractors. That’s what makes us unique.
Unlike most markets, there’s also a lot of political influence advertising here, and that’s a great advertising category for us. There’s more issue money spent here than anywhere.
Advocacy money used to be really big for us, but it’s a smaller part of what we do now.
However, the government contracting side has grown a ton, and we see that as an area that’s going to continue to grow.
RW: Many radio companies are downsizing their physical footprint. You opened a large new facility seven years ago. Do you still need that much space now?
Oxley: No, we don’t. The reality is a lot more people work remotely now.
The tools are so much better. Our reporters, a lot of them do amazing things with just an iPhone with audio and video.
Our remote work has increased significantly. The workflows have changed. Salespeople can work from anywhere. Docking stations and good connectivity means that you can do your job from all over the place with a laptop, let alone your phone.
So if I had it to do over again, we wouldn’t need anywhere near as much space as we have.
RW: How is AI changing how work gets done in the WTOP newsroom?
Oxley: Lots of ways. But we’re being trying to be very careful and thoughtful about it. Certainly, being in the news business, we cannot afford mistakes. We can’t afford misinformation.
We insist that everything that we do has a pair of human eyes on it, and that people are reading it through, proofreading, fact-checking. We’ve got to make sure things are right. If you lose your credibility, you’ve lost.
RW: Do you worry about the future of all-news radio given the massive amount of instantly available information that Americans now have right on their phone?
Oxley: Sure. You’ve got to always be concerned about that. But we’re on the phone, too, for people to consume our products.
RW: There is great pressure to compete with digital platforms. You’ve gone through the digital transition. How do you choose which ones are successful without diluting the original value of the radio broadcast business?
Oxley: It’s a point a lot of people miss. It’s great to go into all kinds of different platforms and all kinds of different things, but you got to make sure you get ROI. You’ve got to make sure that there is a business plan. You can’t just go into it without making sure that you’re also supporting that with advertising.
I think that’s a missing piece for a lot of folks. They go into it and they’re getting tons of hits or tons of views, but they don’t do much because you can’t monetize.
RW: The Federal News Network airs on WFED(AM), which isn’t a highly rated station. Why is the network successful?
Oxley: So it’s not a ratings play. It’s about reaching the right people. It’s reaching government decisionmakers. CIOs for example, really high up in the government levels.
And while we really don’t see that necessarily in the ratings, we do see it in our streaming numbers and our podcast numbers, where we see the number of people who are consuming that product. It goes pretty deep.
These are things that really matter to the upper levels of government, and we know that we’re getting pretty good numbers there. But it’s a niche play for sure.
Sometimes it’s about getting the right thousand people. Sometimes about getting the right six people. Sometimes it’s about getting the right two people. So it’s a different play than broadcast in a sense, but it’s been going really well for us.
RW: You’ve supported the work done by Dave Kolesar with AM HD Radio at WSHE Frederick, Md., formerly WWFD. It’s a full digital-only station. What does the future look like for full-time digital AM and for that station specifically?
Oxley: I’ll tell you, it sounds so much better. I think that it’s something that if you can find the right format, it’s going to be a much better play than trying to just go with traditional AM. I don’t know that it’s necessarily been proven yet, that somebody can make a business out of that.
I still think it’s a viable way to go because it does make me forget that I’m on AM. It’s like I’m listening to FM.
RW: You play music but no commercials on that station. How long can that go on for?
Oxley: It’s more of a public service play right now. It’s more experimental. No, it’s not making a profit.
RW: What is your overall impression of HD Radio, including the extra FM channels? Is it all that you expected?
Oxley: I don’t think it is what anybody expected it to be. I think it also came out late. And adoption has not been maybe as strong as people like. But I’m not sure that everybody knows how to use it, so it’s still a bit of an uphill battle.
However, it is great added distribution, and we’ve found lots of different uses for it over time.

For more than a decade, Surface has been shaped by the people pushing technology further.
Creators rendering complex scenes. Developers building what doesn’t exist yet. Designers moving between ideas, models, code, and content. Makers whose work demands more from their devices because they’re constantly pushing boundaries.
Over time, we’ve learned something important: the people who choose Surface aren’t just using technology for tasks; they’re shaping what’s next.
Today, we’re opening pre-orders for two new devices built for that reality: Surface Laptop Ultra and Surface RTX Spark Dev Box . These new Surface devices bring to life the broader Windows vision for hybrid intelligence we’re sharing today , combining the power of the PC and the cloud to help people do more with AI.
Surface Laptop Ultra started with a clear ambition: How can we better serve the needs of creators, developers, and AI builders?
The answer wasn’t simply a faster laptop. It meant fundamentally rethinking what a high-performance Windows PC could be.
It started with a deep partnership to optimize Windows to take full advantage of NVIDIA’s RTX Spark™ Superchip. We then designed an entirely new device around the platform from the ground up. Mechanical, electrical, thermal, acoustic, material engineers, and industrial designers worked together from the beginning to fully realize the potential of the RTX Spark.
The result is our most powerful Surface Laptop ever, built for demanding creative, technical, and AI workloads.
Designed around NVIDIA RTX Spark, Surface Laptop Ultra unites an NVIDIA Blackwell RTX GPU with up to 6,144 cores, an NVIDIA Grace CPU with up to 20 cores, and up to 128 GB of unified memory. 1
Run AI models exceeding 120B parameters locally, with up to 1 petaflop of AI performance. 2 Move between creative work, development, and immersive gaming without missing a beat. Keep more of your work on-device, with less reliance on the cloud and access to the CUDATM ecosystem and full Windows AI stack. 3
Power only matters if it lasts.
That’s why we designed a new thermal architecture that delivers up to 2.5x more thermal power capacity than our current Surface Laptops. In a chassis less than 18 mm thin and under 4.5 lb 4 , Surface Laptop Ultra was built for sustained performance.
The 15-inch PixelSense™ Ultra touchscreen is the brightest, sharpest, and most vivid display we’ve ever put on a Surface Laptop. 5 It’s designed to empower professionals to review footage frame by frame, annotate designs, explore datasets, and interact directly with their work.
It delivers the brightest peak HDR of any laptop 6 , up to 25% brighter peak HDR than MacBook Pro M5 7 , and the color accuracy creators trust.
The touchpad is 30% larger, with advanced haptics for precise control across demanding creative workflows. 8
Storage is user-removable, so you can upgrade, replace, or secure your own storage. 9
Surface Laptop Ultra is available in Platinum and Nightfall, so it looks as sleek and sophisticated as it runs. 10
It also features our most complete port selection yet, led by something entirely new: Magnetic Connect, the world’s first built-in magnetic USB-C® charging on a laptop.
The included charging cable attaches magnetically to the right-side USB-C port and releases easily. The port remains fully functional for video, data, and other USB-C devices.
· Two additional USB-C ports
Drive up to three 4K displays 11 . Import footage without adapters. One device. Every connection you need.
Creative professionals get a display they can trust, graphics acceleration when projects get demanding, and up to 128 GB of unified memory to provide headroom for multitasking across demanding creative and local AI workflows.
Developers can use local models with GitHub Copilot to bring agentic coding on device. They can prototype agents, review code, test larger models, and keep development tools running side by side.
When the work is done, the same RTX Spark architecture that accelerates creative and AI workloads also powers a great gaming experience.

articles.title_orig: Different voices, shared challenges: mental health in athletics | FEATURE
articles.title_zh: Different voices, shared challenges: mental health in athletics | FEATURE
articles.content_orig:
Mental health in athletics
It was a fleeting exchange at a press conference, but it touched on a much wider issue.
Speaking at the World Athletics Relays in Gaborone earlier this year, Zaynab Dosso and Elaine Thompson-Herah were both asked about the mental side of elite sport.
Italian sprinter Dosso was clear about the importance she places on it. “It’s very important to speak about mental health,” said the world indoor 60m champion. “You can train however many hours you want, but if your head doesn’t follow then you’re not going to get anywhere.
“Last September I started working with a psychologist. Every single athlete should take care of their mental health because it’s just as important as their physical health.”
The same question was then put to Thompson-Herah. “Coming back from injury has been challenging, mentally and physically,” said the five-time Olympic champion.
“But I’m a tough cookie. I’ve never been to therapy, I don’t believe in it. I’m my own therapy. I do believe in God, though. I also have a supportive team who believes in me, and I believe in myself.”
The contrast was striking. Both athletes acknowledged the mental challenges of elite sport, yet they had very different ideas about how to deal with them.
Across a sport spanning more than 200 countries, there are inevitably huge differences in the way mental health is understood, discussed and treated. Professional psychological support may be commonplace for some athletes. Others may turn first to family, friends, teammates or coaches. Elsewhere, stigma, lack of awareness or limited access to services can make the route to support far less straightforward.
US 800m runner Juliette Whittaker has spoken with remarkable openness about her own experience. During her time at Stanford University, Whittaker won two individual NCAA titles before qualifying for the Paris 2024 Olympic Games. Her results suggested a young athlete whose career was progressing almost perfectly.
Juliette Whittaker in action at the US Olympic Trials (© Getty Images)
The reality was very different. She later described it as the “hardest, saddest and loneliest” year of her life.
After winning her first NCAA title, the happiness had disappeared by the following day. After the second, it lasted less than an hour. Whittaker responded by setting herself another target, believing that perhaps reaching the Olympics would finally make her feel differently. It didn’t.
“I truly believed that if I ran well enough, achieved enough, proved myself enough, I would finally feel enough,” she said.
Instead, her sense of self-worth became increasingly tied to her performances. When running stopped providing the fulfilment she expected from it, she struggled to know where else to find it. After returning from Paris, her mental health deteriorated further. Feelings of emptiness became guilt and shame, and she stopped telling people how badly she was struggling.
In May 2025, Whittaker attempted to take her own life.
Friends found her and took her to hospital. She spent a week in a psychiatric unit and later attended group therapy three days a week, while also taking the longest break from running she had ever had.
Whittaker credits the people around her with playing a huge part in her recovery. “At a time when I had completely given up on myself, I had villages of people who refused to give up on me,” she said, speaking at Stanford’s GameFaces event earlier this year.
“One year ago, I was in a hospital bed with absolutely no desire to live,” she added. “Today I’m standing in front of you.”
Her experience also changed the way she viewed athletics. “Running is a huge part of my life,” she said. “But it is not all of me. It is not the source of my worth.”
After spending so long keeping her feelings to herself, she had learned another lesson: “Asking for help is one of the bravest things you can do.” But asking for help assumes an athlete recognises what is happening to them, feels able to talk about it and knows where to turn.
Research in recent years has examined some of those barriers in different parts of the world.
A 2025 paper on mental health among elite runners in Kenya highlighted the importance of cultural and socioeconomic context. Its authors pointed to issues including the availability, accessibility and affordability of mental-health services, and cautioned against assuming that approaches developed in wealthier countries can simply be transferred elsewhere.
A separate 2024 study involving 20 Chinese elite athletes , as well as coaches and team officials, found that cultural attitudes and sporting environments could influence whether athletes sought help. Participants spoke about issues including depressed mood, competition anxiety and sleep problems, while stigma – including fears of being regarded as weak – was among the barriers identified. Athletes were often more comfortable turning first to teammates, friends or parents than to formal mental-health services.
Kenya’s Wilfred Bungei recognises some of that from his own experience. The 2008 Olympic 800m champion has spoken openly about his problems with alcohol and mental health after his competitive career ended.
Wilfred Bungei in action at the 2008 Olympics (© Getty Images)
Among his wake-up calls were missing important engagements because he had been drinking, and realising that his children were uncomfortable being in the car with him when they knew he was drunk. Looking back 10 years or more, Bungei says alcoholism and mental-health problems in Kenya were often seen as matters of personal choice.
“People with mental-health problems were stigmatised,” he says. He believes attitudes have improved since then and there is now more empathy, although some of that stigma remains.
“The talk behind the scenes doesn’t indicate a society that has fully embraced mental-health issues,” he says. “Most people would rather suffer from the inside than be open.”
For Bungei, his family was crucial in recognising that he needed help. “Family is the first pillar,” he says. “If one’s family accepts that this person is sick and needs help, the individual wouldn’t care much about what society says because they know, ‘I have people who care’.”
He has sometimes compared alcoholism with diabetes when trying to explain to people that addiction is an illness rather than simply a personal failing. “The first thing is accept who you are and don’t care about the noise,” he says.
Bungei also believes athletes need more help preparing for life after competition. “Athletes retire early in life and they have money and plenty of free time,” he says. “Remember, athletes live a strict life 365 days a year as sportsmen and women.”
He says there is still no clear roadmap in Kenya to help athletes cope with that transition. He has, however, since found another role within the sport. Through his work with the World Athletics Media Academy, he says he has regained a sense of “purpose and responsibility” from training as a commentator.
He hopes eventually to use that platform to speak more widely about mental-health issues affecting sportsmen and women in African countries, and what could be done to support them.
Singapore’s Shanti Pereira has spoken about a different kind of mental struggle during the years between her early breakthrough and her rise to the top of Asian sprinting.
Sprinter Shanti Pereira of Singapore (© Getty Images)
After winning the SEA Games 200m title on home soil in 2015, Pereira found it difficult to deal with the expectations that followed. Results stalled, injuries followed and, in 2018, she lost both her Sport Excellence Scholarship and her university scholarship within the space of a week.
Speaking to CNA in 2022, she said that physically she still felt capable of running personal and national records, “but mentally I wasn’t there”.
“There was a lot of self-doubt that kind of grew as the years went by,” she said. At times she lost her motivation and became afraid of performing badly

When can Alexander Zverev climb to the No. 1 spot in the PIF ATP Rankings and become the 30th member of the prestigious ATP No. 1 Club?
Zverev currently holds 9,720 points in the PIF ATP Live Rankings, trailing current World No. 1 Jannik Sinner by 1,230 points.
With Sinner ending his 2026 season due to injury, there are two paths for the German to reach the top spot as early as 2 November.
Zverev would become the World No. 1 by winning the Rolex Shanghai Masters crown and reaching the semi-finals of the ATP 500 event in Vienna.
Alternatively, the 29-year-old would also secure the top ranking by reaching the Shanghai final and winning the title in Vienna.
Zverev first broke into the Top 10 in May 2017 and reached a career-high World No. 2 for the first in June 2022. If successful in his bid to become the World No. 1, Zverev would become only the second German player to reach the pinnacle of the PIF ATP Rankings, after Boris Becker in 1991.
A two-time Nitto ATP Finals champion, Zverev would become the newest member of the ATP No. 1 Club since Sinner in June 2024.

articles.title_orig: In three years, Israel's war on Gaza hasn't just changed the Middle East, it's changed the world | Steve Bloomfield
articles.title_zh: In three years, Israel's war on Gaza hasn't just changed the Middle East, it's changed the world | Steve Bloomfield
articles.content_orig:
A whirlpool of violence has engulfed everywhere from Lebanon to Yemen. Meanwhile, the west has destroyed any political authority it once had
T here was a world before 7 October, 2023, and now there is a world after. For Gaza, for Israel , for the wider Middle East, and for everyone else too. Not all hinge points in history are obvious at the time. Three years on from the day it began, and precisely one year since a supposed ceasefire was agreed, this one is now impossible to ignore.
The before-and-after pictures tell part of the story. An update to Google Maps, released last week , underscores just what three years of relentless Israeli military onslaught has done to Gaza. Satellite images show how entire towns have been reduced to rubble. Mosques and hospitals, visible three years ago, have now disappeared. Meanwhile the once-empty shoreline is now crammed with tents. This is what it looks like when an attempt has been made to destroy a people.
For Israel, too, there has been a before and after. Prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu had cultivated a sense of security, even of impregnability. The ease with which Hamas carried out its terrorist attack, killing 1,200 Israelis, including hundreds of young people at a music festival, destroyed that belief for ever.
Three years on from 7 October, both Israel and Gaza have changed beyond recognition. But the consequences of Hamas’s attack and Israel’s brutal response, which has killed more than 73,000 Palestinians, including 21,000 children, have spread far wider.
Under the pretext of protecting its own borders, Israel has launched wars and military offensives across the region, sending troops into Syria; effectively annexing parts of southern Lebanon, deploying the same tactics there that it used in Gaza; and starting, with the US, an unwinnable war with Iran that has spiralled into a regional conflict affecting all six Gulf states.
The Iran war has sparked a new conflict between the Houthis in Yemen and Saudi Arabia, which this week triggered a mutual defence pact with Pakistan and Turkey, dragging two other countries into the maelstrom. Across the Red Sea, some of the same combatants are involved in the war in Sudan and a fresh conflict inside Ethiopia .
More than a dozen countries across two continents are now entangled in a rising number of wars, with overlapping participants and numerous competing interests.
But there is something else, more insidious, that has changed. The rule of international law, tenuous as it was, has been openly replaced by military might. In 2022, western leaders – building a coalition rightly opposed to Vladimir Putin’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine – made moral appeals based on the violation of international law. In Gaza, they encouraged and supported Israel, even when it was clear that the rules were being broken. That hypocrisy has not gone unnoticed, not just in the global south but among many millions of citizens in the west.
We have watched this happen in real time. Despite the ban on international journalists, anyone with a phone knew what was happening in Gaza from the early days of Israel’s response. Hundreds of Palestinian journalists have reported on the bombing of hospitals and schools, the bombing of cafes and wells, the killings at food distribution points, the deaths of children and babies. War crimes have never before been broadcast in real time, relentlessly, every hour of every day, around the world.
Gaza has also changed how wars are fought. Israel has pioneered the use of AI to select targets, accelerating our descent into a future for which we are unprepared.
A ll of this was allowed to take place in a time when the west could still argue that the “international rules-based order” existed. It may have been destroyed by Donald Trump, but we cannot forget that the dismantling began under Joe Biden. It was Biden who ensured the flow of weapons to Israel continued uninterrupted, Biden who insisted that every United Nations security council resolution calling for a ceasefire was vetoed , and Biden who attacked the international criminal court when it sought to indict Netanyahu for war crimes.
US support for Israel has always been strong and, on the whole, unquestioned. But even Republican presidents have understood they have influence over Israel’s actions and have been prepared to use it.
Ronald Reagan suspended an arms deal in 1981 after Israel annexed the Golan Heights. A year later, his administration stopped supplying cluster weapons to Israel after Menachem Begin’s government used them in populated areas during its invasion of Lebanon. In 2002, the killing of 15 Palestinians in Gaza was enough for Colin Powell, the then secretary of state, to announce a review of Israel’s use of American arms .
Israel was also given a free pass by every other member of the G7, including those run by centrists or centre-left politicians. French president Emmanuel Macron, German chancellor Olaf Scholz, Justin Trudeau in Canada and Australia’s Anthony Albanese all initially gave Israel their backing.
Only António Guterres, the much-maligned UN secretary general, emerges with a modicum of credit. Less than three weeks after 7 October, he called Israel’s response “collective punishment of the Palestinian people” and demanded an immediate ceasefire.
The one ray of hope for the future is that our shared understanding of what has happened over the past three years means that in many countries the political winds have shifted.
Before Andy Burnham even entered Number 10, he apologised for how Labour had handled the early days of the conflict. The UK now has a prime minister who was one of the few western politicians to call for a ceasefire just weeks after 7 October. Ed Miliband’s willingness to accurately describe Israel’s actions in the West Bank as “ethnic cleansing” indicate a change in attitude that could lead to more concerted international action against Israel.
after newsletter promotion
In the US, support for Israel has fallen through the floor. For a Democrat who wants to be president in 2028 there is no credible path to the White House that doesn’t involve support for the Palestinian cause. And yet, we cannot simply close our eyes and hope that a change in America will magically restore the world to how it was on 6 October 2023.
N or should we pretend that the previous era was one we should wish to return to. Did we enter a new world on 7 October, or did we just notice where we were? In the three years before the Hamas attack, the wars in Tigray and Sudan saw many of the same trends play out.
In Tigray, the northernmost part of Ethiopia , a war between the central government and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front killed 600,000 people. There were brutal massacres, forced starvation, widespread use of drones – and absolutely no accountability. In Sudan, too, hospitals have been hit by drones, women have been raped, children have been shot dead. Again, we could see it happen. Again, there were no consequences.
Gaza, though, has undoubtedly accelerated the trend, normalising the immoral. The wars that have begun, that have spiralled out of control and pulled more countries and more actors into their orbit, cannot easily be stopped. There is a momentum to this conflict, a hardening of positions, as each new outrage leads to a response. When there is impunity, when there is no price that those responsible will ever pay, there are terrifyingly few levers to pull. If war crimes go unpunished, they only escalate.
And so a family in Addis Ababa fears the sound of a drone crashing into their home. A village in Lebanon is evacuated, destroyed and the land made uninhabitable. A mundane job at Riyadh airport becomes a daily deadly gamble . A crew of badly paid seafarers pray to their gods as they cross through the strait of Hormuz. The dreams of millions of children shrink from university, fame or fortune, to the brute reality of survival.

articles.title_orig: Flu season is already here. Here’s what to know about this year’s flu shots.
articles.title_zh: Flu season is already here. Here’s what to know about this year’s flu shots.
articles.content_orig:
Walking down the street this week, it may seem like everyone is sneezing and hacking up a lung. But as health officials announce the start of an earlier than usual flu season, how worried should Canadians be? And as we head into Thanksgiving weekend, should we be scrambling to update flu and COVID-19 shots?
Some experts say that while this year's flu season may have arrived on our doorstep sooner than usual, it's not necessarily a cause for alarm — but other experts are stressing the importance of prevention in heavy-hit regions such as Toronto and Calgary, where one of this season's two influenza deaths so far has occurred, according to authorities.
The strain making up roughly 98 per cent of cases in Canada so far tends to be a milder one, according to Brian Ward, professor emeritus at the Research Institute of the McGill University Health Centre in Montreal.
"So far at least, this looks like an H1N1 dominated year, and the years where H1N1 dominates, you can have very large outbreaks, but the number or the proportion of people … who get very sick, is relatively small compared to years that are dominated by H3N2," he told CBC News.
"I'm not convinced yet that we're actually seeing the beginning of a real outbreak. What we're seeing is sort of isolated, small outbreaks."
Doctors say flu season is ahead of schedule this year as cases pop up across Ontario
1 dead, more than 400 confirmed flu cases ahead of vaccine availability in Alberta
But where the flu is striking, doctors say it's striking hard. There are currently more than 400 confirmed flu cases in Alberta, where vaccines aren't yet widely available.
Some regions have started rolling out flu and COVID-19 shots to high-risk populations, with most regions set to offer shots to the general public by mid-October.
According to the latest national numbers, which include data on influenza trends up to Oct. 3, there have been 3,315 detections of influenza across the country since the end of August. More than 1,140 of those cases were detected in the most recent week of available data, showing that cases are picking up.
Influenza has been associated with two deaths so far this flu season, national figures state. The person who died in Alberta lived in the Calgary area and was in the 70-79 age range, authorities say. Authorities haven't yet shared where the second death occurred.
It's an early start to the season. Between Sept. 27 and Oct. 3, 4.7 per cent of influenza tests came back positive, much higher than the average 0.6 per cent rate seen this time of year in 2023-2025.
But much of this national increase is driven by an uptick of cases in B.C. and in large cities such as Toronto and Calgary. Other areas seeing cases creep up include Yukon, the Northwest Territories and Alberta.
"The rest of the country is really very quiet," Ward said.
B.C. warns of early start to flu season, launches fall immunization campaign
He noted that in B.C., outbreaks in long-term care homes are driving the increase in cases, warning that families getting together this holiday weekend could result in further spread.
"That may be the seed that moves the virus … into the schools and universities and marketplaces and so on."
Official figures don't catch every case of flu, as not everyone seeks out a test when they fall ill.
In hard-hit Toronto, family doctor Joseph Param told CBC News the increase of flu patients he's seeing at his practice is mainly among young adults who are more likely to travel on public transit and may still go to work when feeling under the weather, perhaps because they're used to flu season starting later.
You're not imagining it — flu season has started early this year
"Over the last couple of weeks, patients who are very healthy who see me rarely have been coming in with severe symptoms," he said.
"So it is important that the general population is aware that we are seeing … early cases now and so that we start taking precautions earlier than expected."
Doctors advise Canadians to stay home if they feel ill and to get vaccinated as soon as shots become available in their area, particularly with the long weekend coming up.
The protection of flu shots varies from year to year depending on the most dominant strain of influenza in your area.
This year, it's a "good" match, Ward said. Although H3N2 viruses dominated for much of 2025, that subtype hasn't cropped up much in 2026, and this year's vaccine is well-positioned to protect against H1N1.

Flu and COVID-19 vaccinations underway in B.C. as respiratory illness season arrives early
Vaccine-preventable illnesses on the horizon again as Canadian kids head back to school
He said "influenza viruses march to their own drummers" and can mutate even within one flu season.
It's not just flu season in Canada — historically, we see more respiratory illnesses in general cropping up during the fall and going into winter, including colds and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), the latter of which is most dangerous in young children.
About 98 per cent of lab-confirmed cases of influenza in Canada since the end of August have been of the H1N1 strain, according to government data. (New Africa/Shutterstock)
Rates of COVID-19 are currently trending lower right now than last year, with 4.1 per cent of tests coming back positive in the last week of September compared with 10.5 per cent at the same time in 2025.
The National Advisory Committee on Immunizations (NACI) said in September that it continues to "strongly recommend" the latest COVID-19 booster shots for those at a higher risk of developing severe COVID-19, including health-care workers, adults over the age of 65, those with immunocompromised systems and people in long-term care homes.
Several provinces such as Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia are already advising residents that appointments for flu vaccines and COVID-19 booster shots are available now for residents over the age of six months.
New Brunswick , Saskatchewan and Manitoba are currently allowing residents to book their flu and COVID-19 vaccines, with immunization efforts officially kicking off on Oct. 13.
Those living in Newfoundland and Labrador can receive flu and COVID-19 shots starting Oct. 19.
In Ontario, flu and COVID-19 immunizations have been available since last week for high-risk groups, including seniors aged 65 and up, hospitalized patients, long-term care residents and health-care workers, according to the provincial government. They don't open to the general public until Oct. 26 .
In Quebec, you can start making appointments as of Oct. 13, but the flu and COVID-19 vaccination campaign itself doesn't begin until Oct. 20 . It is only free to eligible residents deemed high-risk, meaning non-eligible residents must pay for the shots.
Updated COVID-19, flu vaccines available in N.B. on Oct. 13
Alberta now providing free RSV antibodies to newborns after calls from pediatricians to expand access
Flu and COVID-19 shots can be booked now in Alberta , with the first appointments starting Oct. 19. While flu shots are free to everyone, Albertans who aren't considered high-risk for COVID-19 will have to pay.
In B.C., those registered in their Get Vaccinated system will receive a notification reminding them to get their flu shots. Flu and COVID-19 shots are available starting Oct. 13.
COVID-19 and flu shots will be available at specific clinics in the Northwest Territories this fall, but a timeline hasn't been released yet. Those in Yukon have been able to book appointments for flu and COVID-19 shots since the end of September. No details have been released for Nunavut's rollout as of Oct. 8.
Before heading out to the pharmacy or clinic, it's important to check the requirements in your area to be sure you're eligible and that providers near you have received the necessary supplies to offer shots and aren't experiencing delays.

articles.content_orig:
Jeddah, Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, 10 October 2026 - H.E. Dr. Muhammad Al Jasser, Chairman of the Islamic Development Bank (IsDB) Group, will lead a high-level delegation to the 2026 Annual Meetings of the World Bank Group (WBG) and the International Monetary Fund (IMF), taking place in Bangkok, Thailand, from 12 to 19 October 2026.
Amidst a complex global economic landscape, Dr. Al Jasser will engage in strategic dialogues with finance ministers, leaders of multilateral development banks, and key international partners. The discussions will primarily focus on economic stability, trade resilience, scaling development finance, and deepening regional cooperation.
Dr. Al Jasser will hold a bilateral meeting with H.E. Mr. Ekniti Nitithanprapas, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance of Thailand, the host country.

articles.title_orig: Woman survives pancreatic cancer after routine heart scan catches early sign: "I feel so lucky"
articles.title_zh: Woman survives pancreatic cancer after routine heart scan catches early sign: "I feel so lucky"
articles.content_orig:
Bookstore owner Vicky Titcomb had no reason to suspect anything was out of the ordinary when she went to Mass General Brigham for a heart scan in March 2025.
The 72-year-old Cape Cod bookstore owner and great-grandmother felt healthy. The scan was just a routine errand she had to run before traveling to New York City to visit her son. After the test was complete, Titcomb drove to New York. She didn't think about the scan again until she received a call from her internist on the last day of her visit.
The doctor had alarming news: There was an abnormality on her pancreas. Further testing would be necessary, but she likely had pancreatic cancer , one of the deadliest types of cancer.
"I felt like my life just switched in that moment," Titcomb said. "It was a very weird feeling."
But it wasn't Titcomb's first experience with a scary diagnosis. She had been treated for breast cancer in 2012. Then, she had worried. This time, she decided to stay positive. When tests confirmed she had pancreatic cancer , she made the choice not to research the often-deadly diagnosis.
"I saw some terrible, terrible information about it," Titcomb said. "I shut it out pretty much completely, because it was too much to take in."
Pancreatic cancer is one of the most deadly forms of the disease, because it is often diagnosed after it has already spread to other organs. The 5-year overall survival rate for the disease is 13%. In its 2026 Cancer Progress Report , the American Association for Cancer Research noted that even as most cancer survival rates climb, pancreatic cancer statistics have seen little improvement despite advances in treatment .
In addition to the pancreatic cancer, Titcomb also had stage 1 breast cancer that needed treatment, and a mass on her ovary. The ovarian mass was handled first: Titcomb had the organ removed, and a test showed the mass was benign.
That left just the breast and pancreatic cancers. Cancer specialists at Mass General Brigham developed a plan to treat as much of Titcomb's disease as possible. It would start with chemotherapy and radiation to shrink the tumors.
"I was told the size of the (pancreatic) cancer was about the size of a grape. The goal, to me, was trying to make this cancer a raisin," Titcomb said. "That's the way I visualized it."
If all went well, Titcomb would undergo a procedure known as a Whipple, during which surgeons remove the head of the pancreas, the first part of the small intestine, the gallbladder, and the bile duct, then rejoin the organs to allow the digestive system to function. The operation is complex, but Titcomb was glad to be eligible for it: Only about 1 in 5 pancreatic cancer patients have disease that can be treated with a Whipple. Titcomb's early diagnosis had made it an option for her.
"If I had not had that scan when I did, the outcome would have been bad," Titcomb said.
Titcomb began chemotherapy in June, receiving eight doses over four months. That was followed by three weeks of radiation and more rounds of chemotherapy. Surgical oncologist Dr. Thomas Clancy, who oversaw Titcomb's care, said she tolerated the treatments "very well." The chemotherapy and radiation successfully shrank the cancer, he said, allowing him to schedule her for a Whipple.
On Nov. 4, Titcomb underwent a procedure to treat her breast cancer. Just over two weeks later, Clancy performed the robotic Whipple. The operation is difficult on a patient, Clancy said, though the robotic approach allows for smaller incisions and a faster recovery time. But Titcomb felt confident, because it was scheduled for World Pancreatic Cancer Day.
"I was sure that Dr. Clancy chose me for that day because he felt positive about the outcome, because you don't want somebody to do badly on World Pancreatic Cancer Day," Titcomb joked.
It turned out the scheduling was only a coincidence. Still, the surgery was a success. Titcomb said she was up and walking that night.
After several days in the hospital recovering, Titcomb went home. Two weeks later, she returned for a follow-up appointment. Clancy confirmed she was healing well. But because pancreatic cancer is so aggressive, Clancy recommended she receive two more months of chemotherapy.
"There was a lot going on," Titcomb said. "I just tried to cope with the day-to-day."
After several more rounds of treatment, Clancy was able to tell Titcomb in March 2026 that she had no evidence of cancer. She will continue to receive scans every three months, but his hope is for her to "spend as little time as possible thinking about this."
"She's living her life. I generally tell patients at this point, 'You're done with therapy ... you go about your days,'" Clancy said. "The goal is to not be thinking about it all the time."
Titcomb said she has been trying to do exactly that. She is getting back into the routine of running her bookstore, which family members helped steer while she was in treatment. She spends time with her children, grandchildren, and great-grandchildren. The ones who are far away inundate her with photos, videos and phone calls.
Titcomb is also working to raise awareness for pancreatic cancer and advancements in treatment. She has spoken to legislators on behalf of the American Cancer Society and is working with the Pancreatic Cancer Action Network to share her own story and uplift others.
"I have benefited from enormous advancements in cancer treatment. People kept telling me that 10 years ago it would have been a different story," Titcomb said. "There are advances being made that people who've worked a lifetime on pancreatic cancer have never seen. I feel so lucky. The luck trumps all."

articles.title_orig: The staggering numbers are in on the USS Abraham Lincoln's 321-day deployment: 93,000 nautical miles
articles.title_zh: The staggering numbers are in on the USS Abraham Lincoln's 321-day deployment: 93,000 nautical miles
articles.content_orig:
The US Navy aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln returned home this week after a long and difficult combat deployment. The numbers shared by the sea service for that deployment are staggering.
The warship left its homeport in San Diego in November 2025 and was deployed for 321 days, which included 286 consecutive days at sea without a port call. The lengthy deployment, extended by Operation Epic Fury that kicked off the Iran war, set a modern-day record .
As hostilities began at the end of February, the Abraham Lincoln Carrier Strike Group played a central role in the fight.
The carrier strike group's embarked Carrier Air Wing 9 — a naval aviation force consisting of nine squadrons of F/A-18E/F Super Hornets, F-35C Lightning II Joint Strike Fighters, and EA-18G Growler electronic attack aircraft, among other assets— flew nearly 4,000 combat flights during the 40-day operation.
During the monthslong deployment, it flew 14,037 aircraft sorties and accumulated 31,460 forward-deployed flight hours. An estimated 20.5 million gallons of aviation fuel enabled the air wing's operations, the Navy said.
During Operation Epic Fury, the carrier air wing's mix of fourth- and fifth-generation aircraft launched 1,499 precision munitions, dropping over 1.37 million pounds of ordnance on priority targets such as missile sites, defense production facilities, military infrastructure, and Iranian naval capabilities. Air assets also shielded the strike group from enemy action.
The Navy said that the air wing, with its combination of stealth fighter jets and workhorse aircraft, effectively penetrated contested airspace and demonstrated the "Air Wing of the Future" concept in a real-world combat scenario.
Following the April ceasefire and the conclusion of Epic Fury, Carrier Strike Group 3 supported the Navy's blockade. When Iran began targeting commercial shipping, the group participated in strikes on Iranian coastal defenses and missile sites. It supported a second blockade before finally heading home. Over the course of its deployment, the Lincoln sailed over 93,000 nautical miles, supported by 72 at-sea replenishments.
For its actions during the deployment, the strike group received the Presidential Unit Citation, one of the military's highest unit awards.
Take a smarter break in your day - and see how far you get.
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
The difficult deployment took its toll on the broader strike group, which also included three guided-missile destroyers. Multiple reports indicated that logistical strain caused by the war exacerbated the situation.
Business Insider obtained written responses submitted to Congress by Acting Secretary of the Navy Hung Cao late last month that revealed eight suicide attempts by sailors assigned to the Abraham Lincoln Carrier Strike Group. Cao said that multiple sailors attempted to jump overboard. There were no suicides, though.
Cao wrote that "the men and women of Carrier Strike Group THREE have demonstrated exceptional resolve under demanding conditions," emphasizing that "operational decisions to extend deployments are never made lightly." He said the Navy is committed to preserving crew morale, health, and safety, and overall fleet readiness.
Navy leadership has said that it is taking lessons from the deployment . The service has said that it is loading carriers up with more supplies to ensure self-sufficiency if logistics and support come under stress, adding quality of life improvements, and working to keep sailors and Marines better connected with loved ones.

articles.title_orig: One with the world? A new look at brains transformed by psychedelics.
articles.title_zh: One with the world? A new look at brains transformed by psychedelics.
articles.content_orig:
For about a decade, the mainstream understanding has been that psychedelics cause chaos in the brain. Brain networks—the stable patterns of communication that handle vision, attention, or our sense of self, and more—loosen and start talking to each other all at once. EEG traces get noisier and more complex. “Think of the networks of the brain as highways,” says Devon Stoliker, a neuroscientist at Monash University. “Under psychedelics, these highways break down into many different directions.”
In a recent Nature study, Stoliker’s team designed an experiment to test whether these directions are truly chaotic and random. Researchers gathered 62 people who had never taken a psychedelic before, gave them 19 milligrams of psilocybin, a common psychedelic found in certain fungi, and scanned their brains. Then, they used AI to analyze the drugged and sober brain scans. What emerged was not exactly chaos.
Stoliker thinks chaos is not a satisfactory explanation for psychedelics’ effect on the brain. “It never really explained why an individual would have a meaningful experience, why they might have insight, why they might experience clarity, and why these might translate into positive psychological changes,” Stoliker says. To investigate if there are other explanations, he and his colleagues designed a study called PsiConnect.
Volunteers went through the same four-part sequence twice, once sober and once on psilocybin. The sequence included putting participants in four different settings or contexts: eight minutes of lying at rest, a guided meditation, an 11-minute curated music playlist, and finally six minutes of eyes-open video of clouds moving across a sky. Each participant did all four inside an MRI scanner about 80 minutes after dosing, and again on EEG about 150 minutes after.
There were no cognitive tasks researchers routinely go for in brain studies, but there was a purpose behind this omission.
“We wanted ecological validity,” Stoliker says. “We wanted to know what the brain was like when somebody was having an authentic, uninterrupted psychedelic experience. If somebody took a psychedelic in a therapeutic setting, you wouldn’t have them completing tasks.” Stoliker also points out that there’s evidence that giving someone a task mid-trip pulls them out of the state—a phenomenon researchers sometimes call grounding. “Once you introduce these sorts of tasks, you’re actually interrupting the very phenomena you are seeking to measure.” And it worked.
Half of the participants ranked their session among the most meaningful experiences of their lives, and 24 put it in their personal top five. Stolkier and his colleagues started analyzing their brain scan data to find out why.
Measuring global functional connectivity—how much influence each patch of cortex exerts over the rest—the team found that, when participants had their eyes closed, sensory regions lost sway while associative regions gained. “It seems like the brain’s ability to construct reality, or imagination, or our associations, our beliefs, our sense of self—these faculties had more dominance over sensory areas,” Stoliker says, stressing that the interpretation is a hypothetical. “This could help explain why people have meaningful, complex imagery experiences, why they have mystical experiences with imagery that is personally relevant to them.”
Another observation the team made was that connections within each brain network weakened, connections between networks strengthened. The brain’s modularity, a parameter that describes how cleanly neurons stay sorted into specialist teams, dropped across all four parts of the experimental sequence.
What’s more, researchers found that, when sober, activity in a brain with its eyes shut looked very different from a brain watching a movie. Under psilocybin, that difference nearly evaporated. In the visual network, the gap between eyes-open and eyes-closed connectivity shrank by 85 percent. The results from the EEG session independently confirmed that, with alpha-band activity (normally a marker of the brain gating visual input) reduced by nearly half.
“When somebody takes a psychedelic and they’re able to close their eyes and see complex imagery, there seems to be less boundary between the internal and external world than we ordinarily experience,” Stoliker says.
Regardless of these details, the results rather accurately reproduced the chaos in the brain so many researchers claimed psychedelics caused. This chaos, though, turned into order when the team processed their data in a slightly unorthodox way.
Scientists usually do two acts of averaging in a standard brain imaging study. The first is averaging over time. An eight-minute brain scan comprises a few hundred successive images of the whole brain. To understand how two specific regions work together, researchers conventionally average all these images down to a single number describing how well the two regions’ activity matched up across the whole eight minutes.
The problem with this analysis is that it runs the risk of missing ordered structures that appear for a brief period and then disappear into chaos.
The second analysis is averaging over people. Having produced one such number per participant, the standard approach then pools all of them into a group average, on the assumption that individual differences are noise that will be canceled out. Stoliker’s study was focused on individual experiences, so he wanted to avoid that.
Instead, the team fed the moment-by-moment activity of 332 brain regions into CEBRA, a machine-learning tool that compressed the data down to its essential structure while preserving the order of events. For each individual, it produced a trajectory—a path traced through a three-dimensional space, one point for each moment of the scan.
“When they’re not under psilocybin, the brain activity is less differentiated by context,” Stoliker says. “But under psilocybin, we see that the activity becomes organized across time and more clearly differentiated by context.” The trajectories separated into four distinct clusters corresponding to rest, meditation, music, and the movie. A classifier could read a moment of brain activity and say which one the person was in.
It turned out the performance of that classifier scaled with how profound the participants described their experience as being.
To find out which parts of the brain were doing the work, the team replaced one network’s psilocybin activity with its sober version and checked how badly the classifier degraded. The default mode network and the visual network each accounted for over 20 percent of the effect. “The default mode network is strongly associated with the sense of self: daydreaming, mind wandering, thinking about yourself. It’s often been called the narrative self,” Stoliker explains. “On the other end of this gradient, more externally oriented, is the visual system.”
Under psilocybin, the two became less differentiated, which the team thinks explains why participants reported a subjective experience of the self and the external world becoming less separate, a state Stoliker calls “embeddedness.”
“Theoretically, we could suggest that psychedelics are temporarily altering the organization of brain networks that ordinarily help maintain this separation that we experience,” he says. “It really challenges the idea of whether the internal world and external world are separate and highlights the idea that the brain may be responsible for constructing both.”
The day after the session, participants rated whether various things had shifted, like sense of connection to themselves, to others, to nature, along with peace, acceptance, and creativity, all on a scale running from –100 to 100. “For the vast majority of our participants, we found they had positive psychological changes the next day,” Stoliker says. articles.title_orig: Scientists Detect Record-Breaking Radio Signal from the Ancient Universe
articles.title_zh: Scientists Detect Record-Breaking Radio Signal from the Ancient Universe
articles.content_orig:
Welcome back to the Abstract! Here are the studies this week that spotted a blast from the past, opened a portal between realms, yakked it up, and rose from the ashes.
First, scientists have spotted a mysterious radio signal from the primordial universe that could illuminate cosmic evolution (it’s not aliens… sorry). Then: a diamond in the quantum rough, the decline of a fine bovine line, and a second-generation planet.
As always, for more of my work, check out my book First Contact: The Story of Our Obsession with Aliens , or subscribe to my personal newsletter The BeX Files .
Caleb, Manisha et al. “A fast radio burst at redshift 2, three billion years after the Big Bang.” Science.
Scientists have discovered the most distant fast radio burst (FRB), a type of mysterious radio flare from space. This burst erupted when the universe was only three billion years old and sent radio waves across 10 billion light years before they reached Earth on March 4, 2024.
The distant signal, known as FRB 20240304B, hails from an ancient galaxy beyond “redshift 2,” which means it originated more than twice as far as the next-farthest known FRB. Redshift, represented by the variable “z,” measures how wavelengths of light get stretched out in their journeys across space, a phenomenon that shifts them to the red end of the spectrum. Generally speaking, the more distant the object from Earth, the higher the redshift.
“Approximately one hundred FRBs have identified host galaxies with measured redshifts, with the vast majority at redshifts z ≲ 0.5,” said researchers led by Manisha Caleb of the Sydney Institute for Astronomy. “Only a small number of FRB host galaxies have been identified at z ≳ 1. This observational bias is driven by the sensitivity limit of radio observations that are capable of detecting FRBs and localizing their coordinates.”
Caleb and her colleagues were able to capture the remote flash using South Africa’s MeerKAT radio telescope. Follow-up observations with the James Webb Space Telescope pinpointed “a low-mass, clumpy, starforming galaxy” at redshift 2.148 as the host of the burst.
FRBs produce incredibly energetic radio pulses, but the exact mechanisms that generate them remain unknown. Given the diverse features of these bursts—for instance, some repeat, and some are one-offs—they might come from many different sources. In the case of FRB 20240304B, the team speculated that the burst is a magnetar, the highly magnetized remains of a massive star that went supernova.
“The low stellar mass, active star formation, and low metallicity of the host galaxy are consistent with a magnetar origin of the FRB,” the researchers concluded.
This milestone detection of such a distant and ancient FRB opens up the possibility of finding more bursts at high redshifts. In addition to pushing the limits of observation, future discoveries could allow scientists to extract clues about the evolution of the universe that become imprinted in these signals during their vast journeys. So bring on the bygone bursts!
Nayak, Anshuman et al. “Spin force from a nitrogen-vacancy ensemble drives a 100-mg levitated resonator.” Science Advances.
Time to shrink down from the largest cosmic scale to the tiny quantum realm. In a new study, scientists report that they successfully moved a centimeter-scale diamond with a force known as quantum spin, making it by far the largest object ever manipulated by a quantum effect. It represents a major breakthrough, as the diamond is the first object large enough to be subject to gravity to be moved in this way, further bridging the gap between the loopy quantum realm and regular, everyday physics.
A graphical representation of the observed movements. a) When the laser is off, the diamond slab has a small magnetic moment (blue arrow) induced by the latent spin-state inside the nitrogen-vacancy centers of the diamond. b) When the green laser is on, the spin-state is polarized, causing the magnetic moment to fluctuate weakly, pushing the diamond down towards the magnetic field (red arrows). Image: Nayak et al., 2026
In the new work, scientists worked with a nitrogen-vacancy (NV) diamond containing electrons with “spin,” a form of angular momentum on the quantum scale. Then, they shot a laser at the diamond—as science often demands—which stimulated electrons to spin in a certain state that eerily moved the diamond.
“Experimentally observing this spin force for anything larger than atomic scales has proved challenging,” said researchers led by Anshuman Nayak of the Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology. “We have demonstrated the motional driving of a massive diamagnetically levitated mechanical oscillator by the force of NV spins in a gradient magnetic field.”
Congratulations, humanity: We just earned our license to quantum-motionally drive. Proceed responsibly.
Oppenheimer, Jonas and Gillardet, Alexandre et al. “Ancient genomes reveal an extinct bovine species from mid-latitude Asia.” Current Biology.
Domestic cows are overwhelmingly the most common bovine species on Earth today, but this family of swole ungulates once contained a diversity of wild lineages that included aurochs, steppe bison, and oxen.
Now, scientists have discovered the remains of a distinct bovine species—named “yak X”—in Siberia’s Denisova Cave, which was also inhabited by many human species (hominins) during the Pleistocene era, which ended 12,000 years ago.
Yak X (cool name!) began diverging from extant yaks about 400,000 years ago, and had formed its own unique yak pack by 250,000 years ago, reports a team that sequenced its ancient genomes. The youngest bones from this mysterious animal date back about 27,200 years, so it must have died out sometime after.
“Yak X is a Pleistocene megafaunal species previously unknown to genomics,” said researchers co-led by Jonas Oppenheimer and Alexandre Gillardet of Stockholm University. “Yak X appears to have become genetically isolated from other bovines including bison and aurochs despite their apparent geographic proximity in Pleistocene mid-latitude Asia. This lack of gene flow is in notable contrast to hominins at Denisova Cave, which displayed complex patterns of admixture among multiple divergent lineages.”
In other words, hominins at this cave, including Neanderthals and Denisovans, appear to have interbred, while this yak didn’t cross with its fellow bovine relatives. This has been Yak News.
Williams, Jamie T. et al. “Discovery of a second-generation planet candidate accreting onto a white dwarf.” Nature Geoscience.
Planets are frequently obliterated by the explosive deaths of their stars, but they can also be born out of those same stellar ashes. Scientists have now directly observed the first evidence of one of these so-called “second-generation” planets that formed around a type of dead star called a white dwarf.
Located about 270 light years from Earth, the white dwarf—known as HS 0209+0832—was once a star similar to the Sun. About five million years ago, it shed its red giant shell and collapsed into its current husk state.
Since its transition to the afterlife, a new planet has coalesced out those ejected embers, though this world is destined for an early grave. Scientists spotted telltale signs of second-generation elements—including zinc, copper, and niobium—in the spectrum of the white dwarf, which are distinct from first-generation planetary ingredients, such as the silicon and iron that make up Earth. The discovery exposes a dead star feeding on its posthumous offspring that was birthed from its own ghostly gas.

articles.title_orig: Ongoing lawsuits allege GLP-1s can cause serious harm. But we don't know how often
articles.title_zh: Ongoing lawsuits allege GLP-1s can cause serious harm. But we don't know how often
articles.content_orig:
Shelley and Todd Engel. The Engel family hide caption
Todd Engel had operated heavy machinery, like forklifts and rubber-tire loaders, around warehouses and highways in suburban Maryland for four decades.
In early 2023, Engel's doctor put him on Ozempic, a GLP-1, for diabetes. That winter, on New Year's Eve, Engel woke up feeling as if a patch covered his right eye: "I couldn't see anything. It was all dark. It was black."
The doctor told Engel and his wife Shelley it was a form of optic neuropathy — NAION , for short – an inoperable condition caused by tiny strokes that cut off blood flow to his eye. When the doctor listed all known causes, Shelley Engel specifically asked about Ozempic. "'We have heard nothing about that,'" she recalls the doctor telling her.
Seven months later, the journal JAMA Ophthalmology did publish research showing higher rates of NAION among diabetic patients taking Ozempic, or semaglutide, as the active ingredient name is known. But neither Engel nor his doctor were aware, so Engel kept taking weekly shots until his left eye went black, just as the other had done the year prior.
More than one in 10 Americans are taking a GLP-1 drug for weight loss, according to a recent Gallup analysis, and one in seven has taken them at some point. The drugs are prescribed for a growing number of conditions and come with a range of side effects.
Engel has filed a lawsuit alleging the maker of Ozempic, Novo Nordisk, failed to warn patients and doctors about the risk of NAION.
His suit is part of two main ongoing consolidated lawsuits alleging life-threatening or life-altering harm from GLP-1 drugs.
In a statement to NPR, spokespeople for Novo Nordisk pointed to subsequent research casting doubt on whether their GLP-1 drug causes NAION, for example, and said the cases are without merit.
Want the latest stories on the science of healthy living? Subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter .
The legal question before the courts hinges in part on whether the GLP-1 drugs caused the harm. Observational data can show correlation — that people taking GLP-1s were perhaps more likely to have this eye complication occur — but not causation. For that, more detailed investigation is needed.
When the JAMA Ophthalmology study came out showing the correlation between NAION and diabetic patients on Ozempic or semaglutide, two medical groups critiqued it . The American Academy of Ophthalmology and the North American Neuro-Ophthalmology Society issued their own consumer clarification saying, in part: "This is not the type of study that can show the treatment caused NAION." The groups did acknowledge there is a potential link, but further research would be necessary to determine that. For now, they don't recommend that patients stop taking their GLP-1s.
The Food and Drug Administration keeps a database tracking adverse events . It's one of the only mechanisms for doctors, patients and drug companies to submit reports of complications possibly linked to pharmaceuticals. Reporting is mostly voluntary and the agency does not verify the reports, but it is a crucial first step to prompt regulators to do further research and eventually decide, for example, if labels need updating.
In this database, NPR found more than 1,000 reports of optic neuropathy linked to GLP-1s since 2024. That's out of nearly 190,000 reports made about the drug over that period, most of which included minor gastrointestinal issues, dosing errors or injection site redness.
Spokespeople for Novo Nordisk — maker of Ozempic and Wegovy — say NAION and other serious conditions are exceedingly rare in clinical trials. The company continues to collect and share data with the FDA about the side effects reported with the drug since going to market, but the agency has not requested warning-label changes. The FDA said in an email to NPR it has undertaken its own study to assess NAION risks, and is assessing claims and will "determine the need for regulatory action" once its assessment is complete.
That is not sufficient for patients today, says attorney Jonathan Orent, a lead court-appointed attorney on the two major multi-district litigation lawsuits alleging harms from GLP-1 drugs. He says drug makers ought to update warnings to doctors and patients — as they have in Europe — even if the conditions are rare.
It's necessary, Orent says, because "you're never going to have the population size to detect rarer events in a clinical trial; you're also never going to have the diversity of your real world population."
Orent's cases include 247 plaintiffs with NAION, and more than 4,000 with other serious digestive conditions like pancreatitis or gall stones. "These warnings would have made a difference in the lives of real people," he argues. In an emailed statement, Eli Lilly, whose GLP-1 drug brands Mounjaro and Zepbound contain the active ingredient tirzepatide said it will "vigorously defend against these claims."
NPR's analysis of the FDA's adverse events data show 1,928 reports of pancreatitis since 2024. (Other forms of pancreatitis are also listed, including 135 cases of necrotizing pancreatitis.)
Engel says he would've stopped taking Ozempic had he known that it might have put him at risk for blindness. Now, he mourns all he's lost, including the ability to work or walk the beach unaided. "Being able to play ball … with my grandchildren, I can't do these things anymore," he says. "I will never, never be able to see my wife's beautiful face every day."
Obesity and diabetes are complex metabolic diseases that affect many organs, and increase risks for other ailments. That's part of what makes it hard to pinpoint whether problems that patients encounter on GLP-1 drugs are caused by the drugs themselves.
That's part of why Emory University diabetes specialist Mohammed Ali, for example, did not report any of the three patients he's treated who developed serious problems, like pancreatitis or gallstones, while taking GLP-1s, to the FDA's adverse events database.
He says he wasn't certain those problems were caused by the drugs themselves, even if the timing was suspicious.
"They may have had subclinical disease," Ali says. "In other words, we didn't know they had preexisting pancreatitis or preexisting gallstones."
The boom in online sales, where GLP-1s are heavily marketed, also adds to the challenge, says pharmacist Robert Miller at the West Texas Poison Control Center.
Buying drugs on Instagram? "That's definitely a new thing," Miller says, and many sites offer little to no medical supervision of patients. That's why, he says, more calls are coming into poison-control centers like his, with patients reporting vomiting or other GLP-1 side effects.
"So is there even a physician who's motivated to report side effects or someone the patient feels they can report those side effects to?" he says.
These questions are playing out now in court, where plaintiffs like the Engels are seeking damages from drugmakers.
But Shelley Engel also wants more side-effect warnings, which she says might've helped her husband avoid blindness. She says her husband's outgoing, vivacious personality has changed
"This could have been prevented, if we only knew," she says.

articles.title_orig: From tax to slack: this World Mental Health Day, reclaim cognitive space in the era of machine speed
articles.title_zh: From tax to slack: this World Mental Health Day, reclaim cognitive space in the era of machine speed
articles.content_orig:
We challenge you to read this entire article from the top—no AI summaries, no skim-reading headlines.
We are navigating a silent, profound redefinition of what it means to work, lead, and live. In this hyper-accelerated era, we are flooded with endless streams of content, notifications, and automated drafts. We are constantly informed, but are we still thinking?
By trying to match machine speed, we are pushing the human operating system to its absolute limit — a tension I explored while recently moderating a panel with three researchers on the subject. We face a converging storm: overwhelming data volume, always-on intake, the cognitive tax of context-switching, and “AI sycophancy”—where tools are engineered to agree with us rather than push us. To survive this, we crave cognitive counterweights: deliberate synthesis, ruthless prioritization, and active recovery. Staying pace in this environment requires far more than a “moment” for mental health.
The scale of this digital deluge is staggering. Dr. Gloria Mark of UC Irvine, author of Attention Span, found that screen attention spans have plummeted from 2.5 minutes in 2004 to just 47 seconds today. This is not a failure of personal willpower; it is a structural crisis with a measurable cost. Within the Microsoft 365 suite alone, workers are interrupted every two minutes. Microsoft’s Alexia Cambon calls this a constant “consumption tax.” These constant interruptions wear down our goal-oriented minds, forcing us into rapid attention-switching that spikes stress and drives errors.
The risk isn’t the technology itself; it is our desperate pressure to match its speed. Driven by “productivity guilt,” we use AI to churn out highly polished but low-value communications—doing “more” simply because we can. This loop traps us, backfilling saved time with even more low-value complexity rather than freeing up space for deep thinking.
Used well, AI frees us for deeper work, but the courage to make creative leaps must still come from us. Innovation requires creative friction—people disagreeing, debating, and pushing boundaries. This is the exact opposite of an AI engineered to make us feel, as Cambon notes, “nice and comfy and cozy.”
The old innovation playbook of “move fast and break things” is broken. Anne Morriss, co-author of Move Fast and Fix Things, argues that the old way is:
“Not good for people. It’s not actually good for business… [it leads to] more rework, more unhappy customers, fewer people bought in. So, when we talk about how to get this right, we talk about moving fast and fixing things.”
To protect our stamina, leaders must intentionally build a counterweight to modern speed. High-trust, high-functioning organizations deliberately slow down at critical moments. As Morriss observes:
“It’s called good friction… You can go as fast as the amount of trust that you have built… The Navy SEALs have a mantra that I love: slow is smooth, and smooth is fast.”
This distinction is what separates mere management from true leadership. We must set deliberate, not default, priorities and give them our undivided presence. To navigate this acceleration, leadership must shift from rigid hierarchies to horizontal agility—partnering across boundaries to follow the fluid flow of value. Let AI carry the speed of synthesis so humans can bring the depth of judgment.
Furthermore, our most vital qualities—critical thinking, curiosity, creativity, and focus—are products of time and space, not speed. Deep thinking requires “cognitive slack”; without it, we default to pattern recognition instead of original thought. Even Albert Einstein famously sat in quiet rooms for hours staring at the ceiling, knowing his breakthroughs came from stillness, not the rush of the laboratory.
To build intellectual stamina, we must treat our minds like elite athletes, recognizing that peak performance demands deliberate recovery. This requires what Dr. Mark calls yohaku no bi—the Japanese expression for the beauty of empty space:
“To really be able to shine, to do our best work, we have to give ourselves space.”
How we frame this shift matters. Cambon found that mandated “AI-first” processes actually make employees eight times more likely to produce no work at all. The better path treats technology as an invitation to “co-build, co-produce, and co-innovate.” Crucially, Morriss urges leaders to reject an automated, anxious future:
“We have to tell an alternative story — not just the downside and the anxiety of this revolution, but also what could happen…”
For the first time in history, five generations are navigating a workplace transition together. We have a unique opportunity to pair the wonder of youth with the wisdom of experience. True leadership is about consciously preserving the space where original human thought can breathe, connect, and thrive. When managing our work, our teams, our autonomous agents, and our days, we must protect not only the quality of our output, but also the quality of our lives.
As leaders and teammates, we must start with individual actions to reclaim this space. Personally, I have committed to an “analog hour”: handwritten notes, reading on paper, and walking without headphones.
You can also take Anne Morriss’s practical advice:
“Call a friend or loved one on your way to work, or on your way into your home office, and remind yourself who you are outside of that work identity — which… will help you put boundaries around work in a much more productive way.”
Protecting your intellectual stamina is a personal practice, but it also requires collective action. This month, Project Healthy Minds—the leading mental health tech nonprofit expanding access to services across the U.S.—launched the Project Healthy Minds Workforce Lab.
This is a first-of-its-kind coalition of global organizations, scholars, and thought leaders working to expand the evidence base for “what works” in workforce mental health. I am proud to co-chair the Lab alongside Jacqui Canney, Chief People & AI Enablement Officer of ServiceNow .
Together, we are designing the playbook for a future where technology amplifies human potential without exhausting human capacity. We invite you to join us in this critical work—because in an era of machine speed, the ultimate competitive advantage is human depth.
