articles.title_orig: From hunger to hope: Lettie's story on World Porridge Day
articles.title_zh: From hunger to hope: Lettie's story on World Porridge Day
articles.content_orig:
When Mary's Meals first met Leticia, known to many as Lettie, she was 11 years old. Recently orphaned and hungry, she had been forced to leave school and care for her two younger brothers. Her story was first shared in Child 31 , the award-winning 2012 documentary that introduced audiences around the world to the reality of child hunger in Malawi. Now, more than a decade later, Mary's Meals has returned to Lettie's story.
Their new documentary, Lettie , shares a new, very different chapter of her life.
Today, Lettie is an educated, working mother. She works for Mary's Meals Malawi, where she also serves as a Youth Ambassador, sharing the stories of children who, like her, receive a daily meal at school. Her son is thriving and neither he nor his mother are facing the hunger that once threatened to define her and her brothers' futures.
For Angela Chipeta-Khonje, Country Director of Mary's Meals Malawi, Lettie's story is both extraordinary and deeply familiar. "She is one of those children who went through hunger, but she overcame it thanks to a meal that she was getting every day at school". However, Chipeta-Khonje notes, the significance of her story goes beyond survival. "It is a story that is giving hope to so many other children in Malawi," she explains. "And it helps people understand the extent to which children are living in these situations."
World Porridge Day, marked each year on 10 October, draws attention to the importance of school meals in tackling childhood hunger and improving access to education. The day is closely associated with the work of Mary's Meals, which provides nutritious meals to children in some of the world's poorest communities. Although the documentary was released earlier this year, Lettie's story offers a reminder of the lasting difference that a daily meal can make in a child's life.
For children in Malawi, the challenges of hunger and food insecurity are particularly acute. According to the World Food Programme, 6.8 million people in the country are experiencing insufficient food consumption. Most families rely on smallholder farming and rain-fed agriculture, leaving them especially vulnerable to droughts, flooding and other climate-related shocks.
"Food insecurity has remained a significant challenge," Chipeta-Khonje explains. "Most families have been unable to recover from repeated climatic shocks and do not have adequate food production." Children are often the first to bear the consequences. Yet, in the midst of these challenges, a simple meal can become something far greater than food. Mary's Meals "is meeting immediate hunger needs," Chipeta-Khonje says, "but it is also providing the incentive and energy for education, which ultimately breaks the cycle of poverty."
Mary's Meals began serving school meals in Malawi in 2003. What started with around 200 children in a single school has grown into the charity's largest programme worldwide. Today, more than 1.3 million children receive a meal every school day across Malawi. They now operate in 16 countries worldwide. According to the organisation's 2025 impact study, 97 per cent of teachers reported improvements in literacy and numeracy linked to better attendance and reduced hunger. Every teacher surveyed reported reduced dropout rates and improved retention among pupils receiving school meals.
Chipeta-Khonje says these outcomes reveal something important. "Yes, we are alleviating hunger," she says. "But at the same time, it is an investment in human capital development." Education, she argues, is one of the most effective ways of addressing the challenges many African countries continue to face. "We need a population that is educated so that we can deal with the challenges we are seeing every day."
Lettie's story has captured international attention because her journey was documented. But Chipeta-Khonje insists that "there are so many Letties out there".
Over the last two decades, millions of children have passed through Mary's Meals programmes in Malawi. Many have returned years later to share how a daily meal at school enabled them to remain in education, find employment, support their families and build better futures. For Chipeta-Khonje, these stories reveal the true power of school feeding programmes. "They create conditions for hope," she says. "They create opportunity. They bring lasting change that is carried into adulthood and passed on to the next generation."
Chipeta-Khonje hopes that as people watch Lettie all across the world, they will see more than one woman's journey. She hopes they will recognise what can happen when people choose to respond to hunger with compassion. "It doesn't have to be huge," she says. "Small acts of love can do so much for so many children across the world".
It is a message that resonates strongly on World Porridge Day. Behind the simple act of providing a daily meal are opportunities for children to attend school, receive an education and build a better future. Stories like Lettie's remind us what this means in practice. Often, it means a future that once seemed impossible. As Lettie shows, a daily school meal may seem simple, but for millions of children, it can change everything.

articles.title_orig: The iPhone Duo’s Unfolding Animation Is Giving Z Fold 8 Owners FOMO, but Not Me
articles.title_zh: The iPhone Duo’s Unfolding Animation Is Giving Z Fold 8 Owners FOMO, but Not Me
articles.content_orig:
Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.
When I first got my hands on the iPhone Duo , I admittedly dismissed the unfolding animation that would soon become a highlight of online discourse. I was less interested in the smooth transition as content shifted from one screen to another and more focused on details such as the matte inner display and seemingly invisible crease.
But in the weeks since Apple unveiled its first foldable iPhone, which drops Oct. 23 , I’ve seen countless examples on social media of people trying to recreate that buzzed-about animation on their Android foldables. While the Play Store offers plenty of launchers for customizing Android phones — including ones that mimic the iPhone’s home screen — this appears to be one iOS design element that users are particularly eager to bring to their devices.
Sometimes, you really can’t predict what people will care about most — or the lengths they’ll go to imitate a feature.
The primary phone people have used to recreate the iPhone Duo’s cascading transition effect is Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 , which debuted in July with a passport-size foldable design ahead of Apple’s release . Unlike iOS, Samsung’s One UI interface, which runs on top of Android on Galaxy devices, doesn’t include a folding animation. Instead, content simply transitions from the Z Fold 8’s cover screen to its inner display once the phone is opened about halfway. I never considered this a deficiency until I saw the flood of positive reactions to the iPhone Duo’s fluid transition effect.
To bridge that gap, several creators have posted videos explaining how to use third-party apps and developer tools on GitHub to get a similar effect on the Z Fold 8, with caveats like “ the smoothness and quality won’t be the same ‘” and “ install it [at] your own risk .” (That’s encouraging!) The steps don’t seem particularly complicated, and some options appear to have cropped up in the Play Store as well.
I’ve chosen to forgo installing these Duo-copycat apps on my precious Galaxy Z Fold 8 for two reasons. First, I’m not much of a risk-taker. Second, I’m not interested in imitating an aesthetic element of Apple’s software with a derivative version, especially when the Galaxy Z Fold 8 is a standout foldable device in its own right. While the value of the Duo’s sleek animation has since grown on me, I’m not quite desperate enough to retrofit it onto a foldable phone that’s just as functional without that flourish.
Don’t get me wrong: I think Apple’s combination of hardware and software expertise will elevate the iPhone Duo in a way that merits the attention the phone has received, despite being relatively “late” to the foldables game . But I also think it’s more tasteful for consumers to embrace what each phone-maker does best, rather than shoehorning in a competitor’s feature for something as superficial as an animation effect.
The Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 is one of my favorite phones I’ve tested this year, earning it a CNET Editors’ Choice Award. Its versatile design is optimized for both vertical and horizontal content : I can stream YouTube videos and movies on the 7.6-inch inner display, then rotate it to seamlessly scroll through social posts. The crease is barely noticeable, and the battery easily lasts all day. The 5.5-inch cover screen never feels cramped, while its sharp corners give the phone a highly polished look. And despite lacking a telephoto lens, the Z Fold 8’s dual rear cameras pull their weight, capturing crisp, vibrant photos.
The iPhone Duo shares many attributes with the Z Fold 8, including a palm-size design, 7.6-inch inner display and dual rear cameras. Those similarities prompted Samsung to post a series of salty tweets after Apple debuted its foldable last month, including one that reads , “Let us know when you’re done reheating our leftovers.”
That said, I am curious how app developers might optimize their platforms for the iPhone Duo in ways we haven’t seen with other foldable phones. While the Android operating system spans a wide range of devices and configurations, iOS developers only have to cater to a single foldable, potentially leading to a more tailored and streamlined experience. We got a glimpse of how Netflix is building its app for the Duo, and it’ll be interesting to see how both Apple and other third-party developers take full advantage of the phone’s 1.4:1 aspect ratio in ways that could make its predecessors seem behind the curve in that regard.
“Borrowing” features from each other is what phone-makers do best. Down the road, it’s possible companies such as Samsung will implement foldable capabilities that Apple rolled out first, and vice versa. Heck, Apple’s delayed entry into this space means it had time to analyze what worked well for its competitors before jumping in with its own rendition. It’s just how the industry works.
So maybe the Galaxy Z Fold 9 — or whatever Samsung decides to call the follow-up to the Z Fold 8 — will have its own nifty opening animation. But until Samsung itself embraces the idea, I’ll stick with using the standout foldable as-is.

Editor's note: This story contains graphic images of violence and death.
GAZA STRIP — President Donald Trump promised an end to Israel's war in Gaza after he pushed Israel to agree to a ceasefire and Hamas to release remaining Israeli hostages. The deal came into effect on Oct. 10, 2025.
A year later, however, there's still no international peacekeeping force in Gaza as promised and no reconstruction. Instead, Israel's military has expanded its control to roughly 70% of Gaza, squeezing more than 2 million Palestinians near the sea's edge.
Israel has also continued targeting Hamas throughout the ceasefire. Those attacks have killed more than 1,400 Palestinians this past year, nearly 500 of them women and children, according to Gaza's Health Ministry.
Although the bombings have not stopped, they have slowed down during the ceasefire.
That has given people in Gaza a chance to recover from what U.N.-backed experts declared was a famine in the north of the territory last year. More food is now entering, reversing starvation across Gaza.
NPR's reporter in Gaza, Anas Baba, has been capturing moments of respite and continuous grief over the past 12 months of the ceasefire. Below are a selection of his photos.

articles.title_orig: Vos claims second gravel world title with impressive performance in Australia
articles.title_zh: Vos claims second gravel world title with impressive performance in Australia
articles.content_orig:
Marianne Vos has claimed the gravel world title for the second time in her career. The Team Visma | Lease a Bike rider was crowned world champion in Nannup, Australia, after a demanding race over gravel roads and challenging climbs. With her victory, Vos adds another rainbow jersey to her impressive palmarès.
“This victory really means a lot to me,” an emotional Vos said after the finish. This year marked the first time the UCI Gravel World Championships were held outside Europe. In and around Nannup, the riders faced a demanding 125.6-kilometer course with approximately 3,180 meters of elevation gain.
"I’m really happy to have been able to secure the rainbow jersey here."
The succession of short climbs made the course particularly challenging, requiring not only physical strength but also technical skills and good race management. On the demanding course, Vos once again demonstrated her versatility. “There was more mud than I expected. As a result, there were also some slippery sections on the course, so we had to be careful at times. Rosa was incredibly strong, especially on the climbs, where I really had to dig deep to stay with her,” Vos explained.
“It was a fantastic course here in Australia. I’m really happy to have been able to secure the rainbow jersey here,” the Dutch rider concluded. This is Vos’s second gravel world title. In 2024, she had already claimed victory at the World Championships in Leuven. With this latest world title, Vos adds another chapter to her remarkable cycling career and brings a difficult season to a close on a high note.

articles.title_orig: Sliding Doors meets Biff’s Almanac: City saga stirs up a world of alternate histories | Max Rushden
articles.title_zh: Sliding Doors meets Biff’s Almanac: City saga stirs up a world of alternate histories | Max Rushden
articles.content_orig:
Even New Romantics have a view but this long story will not be cut short amid endless hypotheticals and split narratives
I t’s Wednesday afternoon (UK time) and I find myself interviewing Tony Hadley on TalkSport about his upcoming big band tour. We play a bit of Spandau Ballet, chat about the classics and his career – hanging out with Frank Sinatra and Tony Bennett. In as much as you can deduce in a 10-minute chat on Zoom, Tony seems like an absolute gent.
We do always try to bring it back to sport – Tony is an Arsenal fan, there’s a bit of Arteta, Leeds at the weekend. Tony brings up Billy Bremner and suggests that my co-host Charlie Baker and I are too young to remember him playing. We are, and how wonderful to be called young.
Right at the end I go for a slightly cumbersome question/joke about Manchester City . “And I know Manchester City are top of the league, but they’ll probably be bottom of the league by the end of the season?”
Hadley is a pro. Maybe he’s been waiting for this hardball question about the charges. “You just never know what’s going to happen – the world is a crazy place. I’ve got to add to all the big band songs we’re doing … at the end we do a Christmas catalogue which is great fun as well.” What a sidestep.
What am I doing? It’s quarter to midnight in Melbourne, I’m in my shed looking at Tony Hadley on a little box on my laptop asking what he thinks City’s punishment might be. Quick, put a call in to Boy George. What’s Midge Ure saying? Simon Le Bon has things to say, but they are embargoed until Drive Time.
Perhaps this is Enzo Maresca’s best strategy. The City manager’s only way out of answering difficult questions is to organise a 20-date big band tour of the UK so he can do the Hadley pivot and talk about how he really brings the house down with his spectacular Christmas medley.
It would certainly add to the monotony of every Premier League manager giving us their prepared “I’m a football man and all I’m interested in is football – I’ve got enough things to worry about at Coventry/Leeds/Bournemouth, etc.”
But such is the magnitude of the story that even these press conferences are interesting. For the first time since filming players walking off a bus in big headphones became part of the spectacle, I am interested in seeing players walking off a bus in big headphones on Sunday afternoon.
We couldn’t ask for a more perfect place or a perfect time for this game to take place. Liverpool away. The side City have pipped to the title by a point or two three times since the cheating began. I know two of the titles came after the cheating officially finished but don’t think I need to mention that. What if City couldn’t have afforded John Stones (height: 1.88m) and had settled for, say, Victor Lindelöf (1.87m)? How vital was that extra one centimetre of Stones in clearing that ball off the line against Liverpool at the Etihad in January 2019 ?
The hypotheticals never end. Sliding Doors meets Biff’s Almanac. Nicky Bandini explained on Thursday’s Football Weekly that Serie A has two histories depending on where you stand on Juventus and Calciopoli : “I think that’s the truth that English football isn’t ready for yet. Whatever happens with these decisions, whether they successfully end up appealing things or they don’t, you’re going to have one group of supporters who are absolutely certain they didn’t win these trophies legitimately, and therefore they don’t count, and you’re going to have one group of supporters who don’t care and are going to claim those trophies whether or not they get taken away from them.
“I think that’s the grim future that lies ahead for the Premier League. You’re going to have two alternate histories, the same that happens in Italy, where the number of titles that Juventus has won is constantly repeated differently by different sources because one side or another is not going to accept the judgment even after the final appeals are exhausted.”
after newsletter promotion
I’m minded to side with those who favour stripping City of the titles but not assigning them to anyone else. Not just because it’s fun to see how many people say Asterix. Football just isn’t that simple. If City don’t sign those players, they sign other players. Those other players don’t sign for someone else. Games are different, results are different. Players train in different cities, different managers get hired and fired. People live in different places and move to different countries, meet different people. Different marriages, different children. It’s one thing telling Sergio Agüero that the goal isn’t real, but what about his whole life after 2011? Does he have to redo it all?
And then we get to the reason we fell in love with football: geopolitics. If the sanctions aren’t of the highest severity it’s impossible not to wonder whether anything has happened in the corridors of power, or on one of those benches in Spooks or Slow Horses when two people sit on a bench in Regent’s Park with identical briefcases and walk off in separate directions with the other one. Will the UAE really refuse to scrap investment in a tech hub between Cambridge and Oxford if Manchester City are relegated to League Two? It’s ridiculous that the two are even connected.
And while we all wait for the punishment to drop on a quiet Friday, perhaps during the next international break, City have football matches to play, whether they’ll ultimately mean anything or not. Pundits will say “galvanise” a lot. We will all talk about an “us against the world mentality”.
Who will be the first player to tell Erling Haaland to look forward to Salford away next year? My money would have been on Enzo Fernández until I remembered he’s probably frantically checking whether there’s a relegation release clause in the contract he signed in the summer.
I’d imagine it’ll be hard for Elliot Anderson to spend much time thinking about the possible sanctions while he’s trying to fend off Dominik Szoboszlai and Florian Wirtz. Regardless of the result on Sunday we’ll draw conclusions about what impact this news has had – and we may be wildly wrong.
I do sympathise with most City fans. Perhaps not the guy on a radio phone-in comparing this rule-breaking to Emmeline Pankhurst’s fight for female suffrage. But that complete loss of objectivity is part of the beauty of football and sport – somewhere we all lose all rational sense.
At my most pious I like to think I’d save my ire for the owners. They’ve dragged the club into this, they should go, but even that is an almighty mess to untangle. At the same time, if I were City, would I really swap the journey they’ve given me and these highs for finishing 12th every season for the past 15 years? Am I better than that? Like all moral dilemmas, it’s easy to have a strong opinion when it doesn’t affect you and you’re in a shed talking to a New Romantic.

articles.title_orig: We sold everything and bought a one-way ticket to take our three children travelling
articles.title_zh: We sold everything and bought a one-way ticket to take our three children travelling
articles.content_orig:
Dani and Tom Wooldridge worked hard to transform a 1970s house into a beloved family home after they bought it about seven years ago.
Dani, 39, a nurse, also ran an aesthetics business while Tom, 38, had a construction business. Three children, a close extended family and lots of friends. A happy life.
Yet in May this year, the five of them sold their possessions and home, and bought a one-way ticket heading for Indonesia, with the only things they owned in the world now stowed in backpacks in the luggage compartment.
With Olivia, 12, Morgan, seven, and four-year-old George, the Woolridges are planning to travel the world, with no endpoint in sight, hoping to see every continent.
Five months in, over a video call from the Indonesian island of Lombok, Dani and Tom explain the decisions which have brought them to the shores of south-east Asia.
Both of them had gone travelling for a period of time in their early 20s, a classic gap-year style experience, and had enjoyed taking holidays, particularly to sunny destinations.
Dani said: "It was always a conversation we had but once you start having kids and you've got the mortgage and everything like that it's kind of, 'oh it's not the right time'."
But nearly two years ago, the family took a holiday to Thailand over Christmas.
"We were fortunate enough to have a month over there, travelled round with the kids and obviously they were almost two years younger than they are now, and managed really well.
Tom added: "It all went really smoothly and it was great seeing the kids experience a completely different world to what we'd all grown up. It just felt so great exploring with them.
Dani said that sparked their interest to start researching and meeting other families who had decided to jet off.
"We made lots of lists - lots of positives, lots of negatives," she said.
"Can we do this? How are we still going to educate our children? We had a home, we had our businesses, we had careers. What do we do about all that?"
Once they made the decision, they knew they had to be "100% committed".
Dani thought at first they should rent their house out "so we've got something to come back to" but Tom wanted to sell, and the couple realised they didn't want to leave the responsibility of managing it to people back home.
The boys were excited about the idea from the start but the couple admit it was harder for their daughter.
Tom said: "Olivia was a bit nervous. She'd just started high school in the September and we left in May. She was very apprehensive about leaving all her friends.
"Morgan and George do mention their friends now and again, but they're a bit younger so they didn't have that emotional attachment as much as Olivia."
When they told their parents about their plans, their initial reaction was "why are you selling everything you've worked so hard to get?"
"Most people have got bets on when we're coming back," Dani said, laughing. Tom added: "They've all got a year each."
After selling their house at the start of the year, they lived in rented accommodation for a number of months, before heading to the airport in May for the big farewell.
Leaving was "very emotional", Dani said.
"We were very fortunate that we had a lot of family coming to the airport with us," added Tom. "We'd checked our luggage in and we got to the security gates - that was hard.
"We were so fortunate to have a close family and friendship group as well. They're the people we miss and that's what we miss from back home, the people that were in our lives. Not so much the material things we had."
However once the plane had taken off and the goodbyes were behind them, the excitement started to kick in.
"We remembered where we were going," joked Tom.
Even though they had both been to their first destination, Bali in Indonesia, before, the culture shock still hit them.
"It's just everything. Your senses are just heightened. It's the smells, seeing everything around, it's so different to home.
"We went to Bali 15 years ago when it was a lot quieter," added Dani. "People have said how busy it is now, and it was.
"The first day or two was very overwhelming. Our daughter was still a bit emotional. She was up and down with things and we were all a bit jet lagged.
"We went to Uluwatu first and it has got so busy. Even us walking down a road, I was nervous. Scooters everywhere."
But there were also upsides, Tom said. "The food instantly was amazing. And the people are just beautiful, and so kind. And just to feel the heat on our skin."
They moved to different parts of the island, swapping the beaches in the south to climb the volcanic Mount Batur in the north, and spending time in the cultural village of Ubud inland.
They then went island hopping eastwards across the Indonesian archipelago before doubling back to Lombok for a second stay.
"We were moving around quite a bit," Dani said. "So each time it was almost like that feeling of going home because we were packing up, but we weren't going home. I think it took us months to really think, 'wow, we're not actually going home'."
Leaving the UK behind has not meant abandoning education, Dani stressed.
"Even though we want our children to experience the world and have that kind of real world learning, we have said we also want them to have opportunities. So if they want to go to university and be a doctor or a nurse or whatever career path they want to go down, we still want them to have those opportunities," she added.
They have a "huge bag" full of textbooks and workbooks recommended by teachers before they left and they are following the UK teaching curriculum. Olivia has an online maths tutor, who was previously head of maths at her high school in Rhondda Cynon Taf, and had also taught Tom at the same school.
The boys have a tutor who covers the primary curriculum with them and does English and some science with Olivia.
Although the big downside to their journey is missing time with family back home, Dani and Tom say the cultural experiences and confidence the children have already gained from their travels, meeting such a wide variety of people and having the opportunity to live such an outdoor life, outweighs the negatives.
The family is due to be moving on to Malaysia after spending five months travelling around Indonesia, most recently in Lombok for a second stint, where the children have been attending a world schooling centre - which the couple described as a "lovely routine" with amazing friends.
After bringing "way too much stuff" with them initially, they have given away possessions to locals they have met along their travels and refined it down to two large 120-litre backpacks for the parents and two 100-litre rolling packs including one filled with educational materials.
"The kids will have virtually nothing on their backs, just maybe a really small backpack to get on the plane," said Tom.
"We thought the kids would be excited at carrying their backpacks. Yeah, they're not onboard with that," laughed Dani.
Among the things they have planned for Malaysia is visiting an orangutang sanctuary in Borneo and another longer stop at a world schooling centre to give the children more chances to spend time with peers.
Then they move into Thailand, where both Dani's mum and Tom's parents will make separate visits and after figuring out a good location to celebrate Dani's 40th birthday, will move through Cambodia, Vietnam and the Philippines.
With all that, they have the next year "roughly" planned out. They have allowed for contingencies and emergencies - Tom has already had to fly home once for a funeral - but don't have a firm destination in mind yet once they leave Asia, barring a likely brief visit home to catch up with family.
"We're going to do as much as we feel we want to in a continent and then go to the next one," explained Tom.
"Just keep going for as long as we can, and want to. If at some point we don't want to then we'll have explored a lot of places to pick somewhere to stop."

articles.title_orig: The world needs Ukraine’s grain. Its farmers are running out of reasons to plant
articles.title_zh: The world needs Ukraine’s grain. Its farmers are running out of reasons to plant
articles.content_orig:
Ukraine's harvest season is moving from wheat and barley into corn, soybeans and sunflower, and farmer Oleksandr Chumak has had a strong yield so far. That should be good news.
Instead, after 11 years of growing a range of crops in the Odesa region of southern Ukraine, Chumak has had enough.
Storage facilities across both Ukraine and Russia are filled with millions of tons of produce that would normally be sent to Europe, the Middle East, Asia and Africa — but are instead trapped in the warring countries.
Russian drone and missile hits on Black Sea targets intensified over the summer and into fall, making it impossible to insure commercial ships. Kyiv's retaliatory attacks mean Russian exports are now also stuck, further squeezing global supply.
And with fatal Black Sea attacks continuing into October , prospects of a ceasefire look slim, even as Turkey ramps up efforts to broker a deal due to the risk to global food security.
Chumak says that around 80% of his grain cannot currently be sold at a profit, and he is out of cash.
A collapse in domestic prices is giving farmers like him little reason to sow for the 2027 crop in the coming months.
"For the farmers, it's very difficult because we need to pay taxes, we need to pay rent for land, and now we are not able to do this because we are not able to sell anything," said Andrii Dykun, chairman of the Ukrainian Agri Council.
"The only crops we are able to sell are rapeseeds and sunflower seeds. But still, the volume is not enough... So why should we plant if today we have no profits at all?"
"If our stocks will be full, it makes no sense to do any farm operations in the spring because then it's just a waste of time and money."
PrivatBank, Ukraine's biggest lender, told CNBC that it had disbursed 1.53 billion hryvnia ($34.2 million) in working capital finance to agribusinesses between June and August, more than double the 718 million hryvnia lent in the same period last year. Small and medium-sized producers account for 70% of its agricultural loan book.
"Funds effectively remain tied up in grain inventories, while farms still need to cover their ongoing operating expenses and secure financing for the autumn and spring sowing campaigns," said Yevhen Zaihraiev, chief corporate and SME business officer at state-owned PrivatBank.
"We are seeing different strategies among our clients. Some agricultural producers are selling their crops sooner, even at less attractive prices, in order to maintain sufficient operating liquidity. Others, particularly those with access to storage capacity, are postponing sales in anticipation of more favorable market prices," he said by email.
Ukrainian production of grains and oilseeds is forecast to increase to 85 million tonnes from 80 million tonnes this year, but carry-over stocks from the previous season are pressuring Ukraine's storage infrastructure and logistics, Zaihraiev noted. Those facilities include long plastic silobags snaking across fields and towering metal grain elevators that are themselves increasingly vulnerable to military strikes.
"We are also seeing agricultural producers gradually revise their planting plans for next year in favor of oilseeds and niche crops, whose prices are less dependent on logistics costs," Zaihraiev added.
Farmer Oleksandr Chumak said he will follow that strategy, significantly scaling back planting for next year, avoiding corn and barley altogether, and instead opt for crops which require less fertilizer — which is also facing a global squeeze following amid the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran .
Meanwhile, for Ukrainian farmers — those not currently being drafted to serve — the war with Russia is ever-present. "We are living and working in a place where any time you or your circle can be hit by [a] rocket or drone," Chumak said by phone. "We are sleeping in beds with explosions 300 to 1,000 metres around."
Ukraine's agricultural sector has faced farm takeovers, mines and labor shortages ever since Russia's full-scale assault began in early 2022. International bodies have struggled to preserve its export routes through various agreements, including the collapsed Black Sea initiative and the European Union's politically contentious "Solidarity Lanes."
Now, the situation inside the country and the consequences for global food chains are the most severe they have been since the war began.
Between them, Ukraine and Russia supplied the world with more than half of its sunflower oil, nearly a fifth of its barley and 14% of its wheat in the years leading up to the war, according to the UN . Ukraine is also one of the world's biggest growers of corn, with China and the European Union among its biggest buyers.
Around 90% of Ukraine's main agricultural exports typically run via the Black Sea. In August this year, its grain and legume exports totalled 981,000 tonnes, down about 58% year on year.
The risk is heightened by weakness elsewhere. Europe is expected to have a particularly poor corn harvest and needs larger imports just as its demand for feed remains high. The United States is also facing a weaker corn crop .
For now, better wheat and barley crops in Canada, Australia and Argentina, along with good harvests in the Middle East and North Africa, are cushioning the blow.
The continued blockage is supporting commodity prices outside of Russia and Ukraine, but the reopening of Black Sea ports would unleash a wave of cheap supply that would "flip the market fast... with little warning," said Benoit Fayaud, senior manager for grains and oilseeds analysis at Expana.
A deal which restores Ukrainian and Russian exports could see grains prices in other origins decrease by a few dozen dollars, he told CNBC. "They have such big stocks it will be bearish for the market all over the world," he added.
Prices for Russian and Ukrainian wheat, barley, oilseeds and other products have become so low within the countries that it has intensified the scramble to find alternative routes via rail, road and river, according to Fayaud.
But these alternative routes are "difficult and slow from both countries," he said.
Ukraine's Eastern European neighbors such as Poland and Romania are resisting a push to allow grain to transit through them — even temporarily — due to concerns about a glut destroying demand for their own crops.
Another option via the Danube river has been hampered by low water levels; and a key bridge out of Ukraine has been damaged. There are options to export via the Baltic states and through Georgia by land into the Middle East and Central Asia, but this can only cover a small portion of typical flows, Fayaud said.
Andrii Dykun of the Ukrainian Agri Council stressed that there was no alternative to the Black Sea routes when it came to pricing.
"It would always be cheaper for us, even for the farmers on the western border of Ukraine, to sell the grain to other ports from Black Sea ports because it's much more profitable for the farmers than to sell it via the border to [the] EU," he said.
"So without Black Sea ports, it will not work for us at all."

articles.title_orig: AI disqualification yields new Nikon Small World in Motion winner
articles.title_zh: AI disqualification yields new Nikon Small World in Motion winner
articles.content_orig:
Last month we covered the winner of Nikon’s Small World in Motion video: Ning Xu of Tsinghua University in China, whose video captured tiny cilia beating in the airways of a child with a rare respiratory disorder. But allegations surfaced about Xu’s use of AI while making the video. Nikon launched an investigation and concluded that Xu’s entry did not comply with competition rules. The new winner is Nguyen Nam Nhat of Vietnam with a video of a tiny roundworm and a single-celled organism (above).
According to a BBC report, some researchers expressed concern that Xu’s video had structural abnormalities and that cell features appeared and disappeared in a way one would not see in actual cellular biology. Others spotted what looked like AI watermarks embedded within the source files. Xu said he used AI “to distinguish and visualize features in the reconstructed grayscale images”; however, he denied that AI was used “to generate the experimental movie, the cilia, or their motion.”
Founded in 2011, the Nikon Small World in Motion competition is a spinoff of the company’s Small World Photomicrography Competition, which has been around since 1974. Both are meant “to showcase the beauty and complexity of things seen through the light microscope”—one through still photographs, the other through photovideography, taking advantage of all the technological advances that now allow users to make movies or time-lapse images through the microscope.
The other winners also moved up a notch with Xu’s disqualification. Benedikt Pleyer of Bavaria, Germany, placed second with a video of jellyfish larvae suspended in water droplets; Andrew Moore of Howard Hughes Medical Institute in the US placed third with a video of synchronized cell division in neighboring cells; Patrick Hickey of Hypha Research Ltd. in Edinburgh, Scotland, placed fourth with a video of the dynamics of mitochondria and chloroplasts in Turtle Vine leaf cells; and Igor Adameyko placed fifth with a video of a tiny, colorful sea slug ( Cyerce kikutarobabai ) on the move.
Here is Nikon’s full statement:
After thoroughly re-evaluating the video and supporting materials and consulting with members of our judging panel, Nikon has determined that the winning video did not comply with the competition rules regarding generative AI. Nikon has adjusted the competition rankings on our website to reflect this decision.
This decision is based solely on the submitted video’s eligibility under the rules outlined for this competition. It should not be interpreted as a judgment of the entrant’s professional reputation, scientific contributions, or intent.
Advances in imaging and artificial intelligence continue to evolve rapidly, creating new challenges for organizations across many fields. This event has shown the need for Nikon Small World and Nikon Small World in Motion to revisit rules and evaluation procedures for future competition entries.
The Nikon Small World and Nikon Small World in Motion competitions celebrate excellence in imaging, both scientific and artistic in nature. We value the integrity of each image and video selected to appear in our winning galleries, and remain committed to upholding the standards of excellence that have defined this competition.

articles.title_orig: Measles confirmed in local school
articles.title_zh: Measles confirmed in local school
articles.content_orig:
Measles has been confirmed in a local school.
Eden Christian Academy said Friday that it’s working with the Allegheny County Health Department (ACHD) to stop the disease’s spread after being notified of measles in its community.
Two measles cases were confirmed in Allegheny County this week, on Monday and Thursday. ACHD says both people attend the same school but live in different households.
Eden Christian Academy would not share details about any patients, but said it is addressing the issue across its three campuses.
Actions include communicating with families and staff who may have been exposed, deep cleaning across all facilities and advising unvaccinated or non-immune staff and students about “exclusion periods,” according to public health guidelines.
The school adds that its health records and policies are compliant with the state’s student vaccination requirements.
Pennsylvania’s measles outbreak, which has surpassed 1,000 cases this year, is the largest state outbreak in more than three decades, the Associated Press reports .

articles.title_orig: Amid the challenges of the modern world, Amoris laetitia remains a work in progress
articles.title_zh: Amid the challenges of the modern world, Amoris laetitia remains a work in progress
articles.content_orig:
An Egyptian patriarch, an Indian cardinal, an Australian bishop, a French expert and an Argentine theologian, a married couple from the Philippines. All were present at the first briefing in the Press Office of the Holy See, the varied and universal perspective that Pope Leo XIV wanted to impart to the summit for the ten years of Amoris laetitia .
On the third day of work in the Paul VI Hall, where heads of the Eastern Churches and presidents of Episcopal Conferences, experts and couples sit together with the Pope, some of the participants met with the international media to offer details, ideas, and content that emerged in this event of âlisteningâ and âdialogueâ.
Dialogue, understood as sharing experiences on highly current issues, starting with migration which has separated many families around the world and reshaped everyday life and relationships; then the digital age, which affects the way of building bonds or even simply having dinner; and also accompaniment of new couples after the celebration of the wedding, the formation of priests, helping young people to discover the beauty of married life without âscaringâ them or making them feel under pressure, and closeness to victims of abuse.
In short, the work addressed many themes, many ideas, many experiences already lived or initiatives and proposals in progress. âIt is intense workâ, said Jesuit Father Giacomo Costa, consultant to the General Secretariat of the Synod, who spoke about the methodology adopted in recent days.
That methodology had already been consolidated during the most recent Synods and Consistories, whose sessions were punctuated by conversations, meditations, prayers, testimonies and pastoral experiences on the fruits of Pope Francisâ post-synodal exhortation.
Prayer, in particular is something that âmaybe wonât make the newsâ but is âa fundamental moment to enter the climate of a meeting rooted in prayerâ, Father Giacomo emphasized.
After the âfirst stepsââthat is, the initial forty-eight hours spent âgetting to knowâ, âlistening toâ, and âtrustingâ one another (often for the first time)âwork proceeded in various groups. These groups truly reflected the universality of the Church, with tables comprising participants from China, Poland, Italy, Mexico, Central Asia, and beyond. Each group drafted its own report, which was subsequently shared during the plenary session.
Friday morningâs session provided the âinitial overviewâ, offering a chance to reflect on the âbeauty, challenges, and fragility of families today, and what this asks of our Churchesâ, Costa explained.
The focus was primarily on the changes that have intensified in the decade since the publication of Amoris laetitia . These were not merely ânoveltiesâ but âelements of growing transformationââforemost among them the theme of human mobility, âcited universally by all the groupsâ.
This issue affects âhow we live out family relationshipsâ, touching upon separated couples, grandparents acting as parents to their grandchildren, parenting challenges, difficulties in maintaining bonds or passing on the faith, and interfaith marriages.
All these issues emerged from the stories shared by many of those present in the Paul VI Hall. For instance, Costa noted, âit was emphasized that young people and adults should be prepared to live out their faith in other countries and communities, drawing upon the lessons learned within their familiesâ.
Attention was also drawn to the difficulties faced by many families losing their support networks, as well as the enrichment that new experiences and cultures bring to many households.
The digital revolution of the last decade was also central to âmany stories and experiencesâ. There are also many âcreativeâ initiatives by families who are âorganizing new ways to be togetherâsuch as phone-free dinners for conversation, or methods for staying in touch during migrationâ.
The meeting also addressed the training of seminarians raised in digital culture or coming from âreconstitutedâ families. âHow is their experience incorporated into their formation?â was one of the questions asked. âOne can tangibly sense how fragility becomes a place where God continues to manifest the power of loveâ.
Speaking of fragility, the pastors gathered at the Vatican also acknowledged the fragilities of the Church as a whole.
One of these concerns the âaccompanimentâ of familiesâsomething highly desired and promoted, yet sometimes difficult to implement. âAccompaniment risks becoming a buzzword that unites us in theory but remains to be clarified in practiceâ.
For instance, who actually stays close to couples and their children during crises or in old age? Or, how do we move from marriage preparation to supporting couples throughout their lives to help them live out this vocation?
âAccompaniment is the task of the entire Churchâ, Father Giacomo emphasized; âwe must address it together, from a synodal perspectiveâ.
One point on which everyone agreed was the âpressuresâ many families face today. âAre we, as a Church, adding to them with our own demands?â participants asked.
There was no shortage of accounts regarding the difficulties of the current era: long working hours, violence against women, war, and the issue of âdowriesâ in certain cultures.
âCertain tendencies to idealize can burden families with expectations perceived as unattainable and can scare off young peopleâ. The issue will continue to be discussed in the coming days.
Reflection continues on the highly delicate issue of standing with survivors of abuse and those who have experienced violence. These are people who âneed closeness and their own timeâ, and who must be helped to build âtrustâ in the possibility of experiencing loving relationships and intimacy.
All of this, Father Giacomo Costa emphasized, requires an âextra effortâânamely, taking multiculturalism into account. âShared words can refer to different approachesâ.
The atmosphere is âconstructive, pleasant, and sereneâ; the âapproaches do not conflict, but mutual understanding is needed, as the solutions are not the same. We need a dialogue that allows us to explore different sensibilitiesâ.
Work is therefore underway to ârefine a shared understandingâ and build the kind of âfrank and honest sharingâ called for by the Pope.
The first to take the floor briefly to offer greetings at the press gathering was the Coptic Patriarch of Alexandria, Ibrahim Isaac Sedrak, representing the Catholic Church in Egypt at the Vatican meeting.
He was followed by Cardinal Filipe Neri António Sebastião do Rosario Ferrão, Archbishop of Goa and Daman and President of the Conference of Catholic Bishops of India, who reiterated that âfor us, the family is fundamentalâ. He expressed his pleasure at being able to âhear about experiences and responses offered around the worldâ, particularly from lay witnesses, noting that âthis is important for accompanying our familiesâ.
Archbishop Timothy John Costelloe of Perth, the President of the Australian Bishopsâ Conference (âEveryone calls me Tim... only my mom calls me Timothy when I get into troubleâ), reiterated the point regarding the âpressuresâ families face today. âAs a Church, it is important to ask ourselves how we can constructively address the challenges and opportunities presented by the current situationâ.

The new tattoo ink is activated under UV light.
Researchers have developed a new type of tattoo ink that can be switched on and off with light, allowing colors and images embedded in the skin to be changed and even "erased" without having to go through the painful tattoo-removal process .
The system, which is being commercialized under the name PhotoTat, could eventually give people a way to conceal or change permanent body art. It could also have more practical applications, including medical tattoos that are visible only when a doctor needs to see them, researchers reported in a study published Friday (Oct. 9) in the journal Matter & Light .
"This is a tattoo that you can have, and whenever you decide you don't want it to be showing anymore, or you just don't want it there, you just turn it off," said study co-author Carson Bruns , an associate professor of biomedical engineering at the University of Colorado at Boulder. "And that's it. You don't have to turn it on again."
PhotoTat contains three primary color inks — blue, magenta and yellow — made with photochromic dyes , which are light-sensitive compounds that can change color with different wavelengths of light. These dyes are encapsulated in nanoparticles of polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) — a medical-grade, glass-like plastic that is already used in medical implants and dermal fillers.
The dyes change their molecular structure when exposed to specific wavelengths of light. A 365-nanometer ultraviolet (UV) LED can activate pigments in around two to three seconds, Bruns said. Once activated, the colors can persist for hours to days under typical indoor lighting. But once the wearer exposes their skin to the bright outdoor sun, the colors disappear in seconds, erased by the intense light.
That makes the tattoo unique, as the pigment itself remains in the skin but the tattoo's appearance changes. Bruns and his team found that all three PhotoTat channels remained switchable in the skin for between 1.4 and 2.2 years.
The three colors enable someone to activate different portions of a tattoo using different wavelengths of light. That means the magenta part of the tattoo might be turned on with green light, while the yellow pigment would be activated by blue light. This allows the wearer to customize their design and coloration to whatever they want at the moment — from a purple cherry to a yellow group of hearts.

That feature makes PhotoTat appealing for "people who love tattoos and have lots of tattoos, but just want something kind of fun and playful to add," Bruns told Live Science.
Bruns has tested each iteration of PhotoTat's inks on his own skin. His art is arranged in a series of tattooed scales, with different ink formations in individual scales.
"I gave myself these scales on purpose because they're each sort of a container for an experiment," Bruns said. The result, he joked, resembles a "magical mermaid trick," with some scales appearing out of nowhere and others changing color when activated.
The technology can also be combined with conventional tattoo ink. A permanent black ink design, for example, could contain hidden PhotoTat elements that appear only when activated.
The new tattoos could be appealing to people who want tattoos but are hesitant about their permanence, as well as to people who love their tattoos but occasionally need to conceal them because of work, social expectations or family, Bruns said.
"It's going to be on for most of the time, but just for this one moment, I'm going to turn it off for you grandma, for example," Bruns said.
Bruns thinks the tattoos could be helpful in a medical setting, too. Patients undergoing radiation therapy, for example, sometimes receive permanent tattoos that help doctors precisely align radiation beams. While useful, those marks remain after the treatment, reminding the patient of their experience. These would make such markings invisible if a patient wants them to be.
PhotoTat could potentially allow similar markings to be switched on during surgery and hidden afterward.
Bruns has spent several years developing other smart tattoos for medical applications, including a dosimeter-type tattoo that measures the amount of UV radiation a wearer experiences, along with a tattoo that changes color when the wearer is exposed to dangerous gamma radiation .
A cancer patient receives radiation treatment, guided by laser lines and a tattoo on their skin.
"It's not for you and me, but if you're like an astronaut or a nuclear engineer, they have to wear these dosimeters," Bruns said. "So, we have like a dosimeter tattoo that sort of puts that in your skin."
So far, Bruns and a fellow tattoo artist, have only commercialized the purple PhotoTat ink , after running the ink through a series of third-party medical tests.
The tests showed the purple is safe for use, and available to order, but it isn't cheap at $100 for a small bottle. Bruns hopes as more research is done, he can bring the other colors to market and lower the production cost, so the technology is more accessible.

Elyse Thorpe's daughter, May
[Content Warning: This blog post discusses suicide.]
My daughter loved sloths, black-razzberry La Croix, and olives. Her cosplay character was Noelle Holiday from Deltarune. Her favorite holiday was Christmas. She chose her favorite soft pink t-shirt to die in. My transgender daughter May died by suicide in January of 2026. She was 16, just a few weeks short of her 17th birthday, and she was done with the cruelty of the world. She had the love and support of her father, mother, and brother. But it just wasn’t enough. May wanted the happy, carefree childhood that every child wants, or to at least have no more than the usual cares of school and chores and relationships. Instead, she spent the last years of her life fighting — fighting for access to health care, fighting for access to safe bathrooms, fighting to be treated with dignity. It’s hard to convey the great cost of that fight to a person, especially a child, and their family.
Though she was extremely sensitive to the injustices of the world, she would have much preferred to just be a kid than to be a warrior. Instead, her trans identity put her body in the political crossfire of health care and bathroom bans in our state. She fought back through her participation in the Lambda Legal lawsuit challenging the Idaho’s K-12 bathroom ban, sharing with the courts what it’s like to have a most basic human need treated like a crime.
It’s so hard to protect your child from a world that looks at them and does not see anything of value. My smart, funny, kind kid didn’t want to wait around to see what rights she would lose next. My overwhelming grief is tightly intertwined with anger at a state and a country that made her life, already complicated by her medical needs, harder and lonelier than it needed to be.
We are well into the stage of persecution where silence is complicity. Children like my daughter need their advocates to be pervasive, especially in education and health care, and they need those advocates to be highly visible and extremely vocal. And it cannot just be the LGBTQ community and their loved ones, because they, and we, are exhausted.
A flag or a pin or a sticker of solidarity is appreciated, but not enough. Allies need to remember that the pin or flag or sticker they show as a sign of safety to others is also a pledge to themselves to be vocal and vigilant against any conversations around trans children that are not firmly grounded in an understanding that the safety and dignity of all children comes first. The fear of making adults uncomfortable cannot be greater than the safety and dignity of trans children.
What gives me hope is that we live in a great age of storytelling. Never before in history have we had so much access to the experiences of so many people traveling many different roads through this life. It’s glorious.
Stories, with their antibodies of empathy, are the great inoculator against disinformation. It’s only a matter of time before we reach herd immunity against ignorance and hatred, which may linger but will have no power to spread.
Those who can offer financial support to the legal aid and community aid organizations working to support trans adults and kids are cherished. Those who can offer their time and energy to those organizations and their enterprises are beloved. But we all can offer our attention to the stories of trans people, whether they are shared through memoir, fiction, comic and graphic art, theater, TV, film, visual arts, or simply creating social media content.
My daughter didn’t live long enough to tell her whole story herself. Now, her family and friends share her story in the hope that we can create a world that would have welcomed May with open arms.
If you are struggling and need help, know that there is a community waiting for you with open arms. You are not alone.
